overview:
Unggarrangu is a non-Pama Nyungan language of the Worrorran family, specifically western Worrorran, along with Worrorra K17; Umiida K49; Unggumi K14; Yawijibaya K53; Winyjarrumi K56 (McGregor and Rumsey, 2009:8).

Coate (1970) collected some words and sentences while Capell (1984) presents a comparative study of Northern Kimberley languages including Unggarrangu.
location_info:
Northeastern side of King Sound from east side of Stokes Bay north to Crawford Bay and the eastern islands of the sound from Helpman Island to Caffarelli; not on inshore islands east of Byron Island. On mainland they went inland only for about 10 miles (15 km.) (Tindale 1974).

All islands on east side of King George's Sound (Oates 1975:55). There was no direct information on the territorial associations of Unggurranggu in 2007. Bardi and Jawi owners however agreed that the eastern neighbours of Jawi were Unggurranggu and not Umiide (Bowern p.c. in Harvey AILEC 0802).

overview:
Wakka Wakka is the language of the Wakka Wakka People of the Burnett Downs area, QLD. Wakka Wakka E28 is also used as the name of a subgroup. The name Wakka Wakka follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, wakka means 'no' (Tindale 1974:187). This distinguishes Wakka Wakka from similar neighbouring languages.

Wakka Wakka is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language programs have been implemented, including workshops and the development of language learning resources (see SEQILC 2025, Yumi Sabe 2025). Wakka Wakka language programs have run across kindergarten, primary and secondary schools in and around Cherbourg, Murgon and Eidsvold, QLD.

Wakka Wakka is a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). Wakka Wakka is also used as the name of a subgroup. Other languages in the subgroup are Wuli Wuli E89, Djagunda E27, Barunggam D40 and Giabal D41 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4). Additionally, the Jinibara group (see Dalla E25) is a part of the Wakka Wakka subgroup. Wakka Wakka is also associated with Gubbi Gubbi E29 and Gooreng Gooreng E32 (Kite & Wurm 2004:6).
location_info:
Wakka Wakka is located in southeast Queensland, extending south to the Brisbane River, west to the Bunya Mountains and Boyne River, east to the Jimna Range and north to the Burnett River, Gayndah and Mundubbera (Kite & Wurm 2004:6).

Neighbouring languages include Gooreng Gooreng E32 to the north, Gubbi Gubbi E29 to the east, Giabal D41 and Jarowair E81 to the south, Dalla E25, Nalbo E90, Duungidjawu E20, Garumngar E88 to the southeast and Wuli Wuli E89, Djagunda E27 and Barunggam D40 to the west.

overview:
The Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation web site lists Nharnu among 'some of' the Wajarri A39 dialects, the others being Birdungu A40, Mileura A114, Nhugarn A71, Byro A113 and Ngunuru A112.

Marmion (1996:6-7) does not include Nharnu in his description of Wajarri A39 dialects (MS 4096), but notes that it is definitely a distinct variety of Wajarri, though one that he only heard about after completing his honours thesis (Marmion 2015 p.c.).
location_info: spoken in the far north-east of Wajarri country, in the area north-west of Meekatharra, perhaps up around the small community of Yulga Jinna (Marmion 2015 p.c.)

overview:
Kulkalgaw Ya is the language of the Kulkalgal Nation of the Central Islands of Zenadth Kes (Torres Strait). It is a variety of Kala Lagaw Ya Y1.

Zenadth Kes is a name commonly used instead of the non-Indigenous name 'Torres Strait'. It was created by Elder and linguist Adhi Ephraim Bani, who wanted to redefine the non-Indigenous name by combining traditional names for the four winds that pass through the region (Torres Strait Island Regional Council 2026).

Kulkalgaw Ya is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. One available resource includes Sidney Ray's (2003) Dictionary of Torres Strait languages. The first language program was run in the 1970s. Since 2008, Tagai State College has supported the teaching of Zenadth Kes traditional languages, and has worked with the Torres Strait Traditional Languages Centre to support language revitalisation (Torres Strait Traditional Language Centre 2026).

In 2015 the Torres Strait Regional Authority, Tagai State College and communities across Zenadth Kes formed a 'language reference group' in order to coordinate language revitalisation and develop a Traditional Language Plan (Zenadth Kes Language Symposium 2024). Since then, Community Language Teams, languages programs and cultural activities have occurred in both Meriam Mir Y3 and Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 varieties (Torres Strait Traditional Languages Plan 2016-2019). In 2023 the Torres Strait Traditional Languages Association was established to continue to support and revitalise Zenadth Kes traditional languages.

Torres Strait Creole P2 is a language shared across all of Zenadth Kes (Torres Strait Traditional Languages Plan 2016-2019). The western variety of Torres Strait Creole P2 shares features with Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 (Tudor-Smith 2024:148). Torres Strait Creole P2 is used to identify Torres Strait Islanders in Collections Online. This does not imply that all Torres Strait Islanders are speakers of Torres Strait Creole P2. Sources relating to Torres Strait Creole P2 may be relevant.

Kulkalgaw Ya is a Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 (Western Torres) language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 is the traditional name for the Western Torres language subgroup, which includes the following Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 varieties: Kalaw Kawaw Ya Y2, Mabuyag Y239, Kulkalgaw Ya and Kawalgaw Ya Y5. Waru lag Y227 may be another Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 variety (Laade 1968:145).

The classification of Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 as a Pama-Nyungan language has been debated. It shares linguistic features, such as vocabulary and grammar, with Papuan languages as well as Pama-Nyungan languages. Contemporarily, it is largely believed to be a Pama-Nyungan language (see Alpher et. al. 2008).

Note: Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 was referred to as Mabuiag or Mabuiagic in earlier surveys. Sources relating to Mabuyag Y239 may be relevant.
location_info:
Kulkalgaw Ya is located on the islands of Aurid, Damut, Iama, Masig, Mauar, Naghir, Poruma and Warraber in Zenadth Kes (Torres Strait)(Torres Strait Traditional Language Centre 2026).

Neighbouring languages include Torres Strait Creole P2, Waru lag Y227 to the northeast, Kalaw Kawaw Ya Y2 to the northwest, Meriam Mir Y3 to the east, Kawalgaw Ya Y5 to the southwest and Mabuyag Y239 to the west.

overview:
According to the Kimberley Handbook, Najanaja is the coastal dialect of three Karajarri A64 dialects, the other two being Nawurtu A107 from inland and Nangu A105 in the middle. McGregor (2004:9) says that owners of the Nangu, Nawurtu and Najanaja language varieties regard them as types of Karajarri and use both the general and more specific terms in reference to their language.

Wangka Maya (2012) notes that Janet Sharp drafted a grammar of Najanaja Karajarri, and McKelson (1989) says that Capell, Worms and Nekes have made studies of Najanaja with reference made to inland Karajarri.
location_info: ... located ocean side of Bidyadanga (McKelson & Dodd 2007:191).

overview: Austin (1981:4-5) identifies evidence of there being at least two dialects of Dhirari L14. He says the data in Reuther (1903), collected at Killalpaninna (Northern Dhirari), differs from data originating in Muloorina (Southern Dhirari L70) in terms of vocabulary (69% common) but phonologically the two are nearly identical.
location_info: Killalpaninna (Austin 1981:4).

overview:
In explaining the etymology of the term Dalabon N60 (dalû- 'mouth' + bon 'go'), Evans and Merlan (2003:269) mention that Dangbon N60 and Ngalkbon are 'parallel formations based on the root for 'mouth' in Bininj Gun-wok N186 and Jawoyn' N57, used by speakers of each of those languages respectively.

Cutfield (2011), discussing Dalabon N60, comments that 'Dialectal variation is reported in geographical and social dimensions (i.e. clan lects). Dangbon N230 and Ngalkbon are sometimes used as labels to distinguish northern and southern Dalabon (respectively), two varieties which display a few differences according to Evans, Merlan and Tukumba (2004:ix).
Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre (2012) says Nankilakuthu is one of the four speaker-identified dialects of Nyiyaparli A50.
location_info: ... the top of Nyiyaparli country [Pilbara] (Wangka Maya PALC 2012:ii).

overview: Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre (2012) says Martuyitha is one of the four speaker-identified dialects of Nyiyaparli A50.

Djagunda is the language of the Auburn Hawkwood People / Djaku-nde / Djagunda people of the upper Boyne and Auburn Rivers, QLD. It is a language of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup. There is little information about the meaning of the name Djagunda.

Wakka Wakka E28, which is related to Djagunda, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language programs have been implemented, including workshops and the development of language learning resources (see SEQILC 2025, Yumi Sabe 2025). Wakka Wakka E28 language programs have run across kindergarten, primary and secondary schools in and around Cherbourg, Murgon and Eidsvold, QLD.

Djagunda is a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:4) and is associated with the following Wakka Wakka E28 varieties in addition to the Jinibara group (see Dalla E25) group: Wuli Wuli E89, Barunggam D40 and Giabal D41 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).

Djagunda has previously been associated with Gooreng Gooreng E32 (O'Grady et. al. 1966:50; Wurm 1972:140) and Mbabaram Y115 (Tindale 1974:167).
location_info:
Djagunda is located in the area surrounding Kumbia in southeast Queensland, extending across the upper Boyne and Auburn Rivers, north to Hawkwood and south to the Great Dividing Range (Capell 1963:5; Tindale 1974:167).

Neighbouring languages include Wuli Wuli E89 to the north, Wakka Wakka E28 to the east, Barunggam D40 to the south and Yiman E31 to the west.

overview:
The Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation web site lists Mileura (A114) among 'some of' the Wajarri (A39) dialects, the others being Birdungu A40, Nharnu A115, Nhugarn A71, Byro A113 and Ngunuru A112.

Marmion (1996:6-7) does not include Mileura Wajarri in his description of Wajarri (A39) dialects. Marmion (2015 p.c.) notes that in more recent times Wajarri varieties have been referred to by station names in the area, such as Byro station and Mileura station, leading to some names existing in parallel with older names. He says that Mileura Wajarri is probably equivalent to Ngunuru A112.
location_info: Mileura station (Elefsiniotis 2007 p.c.)

overview:
Von Brandenstein lists Windaga as one of his six 'Dundas District dialects' but puts a question mark after this name. He says it is a tribal name and that he is not sure if it 'belongs to Njagi-Njagi' A1 (which is outside of his 'Dundas district').

There is no language data; consequently, Windaga is not included as a language heading in the Thesaurus.
location_info: ... from Norseman to Peak Charles (von Brandenstein 1980:2)

overview:
Capell (1963) and Oates (1975) list Wadigali as a dialect of Maljangaba L8, based on Wurm, who uses the word 'probably'. Beckett, Hercus and Martin (2008) say Wadikali (L12) is part of the 'closely-knit subgroup of Yarli languages' but they do not mention dialect status. Hercus and Austin define it as a member of the Yarli subgroup, along with Malyangapa L8 and Yardliyawara L7 (2004: 207-8).

The Mobile Language Team web site locates Wadigali to the 'north of the closely related language / dialect Malyangapa'.

Oates and Oates (1970) note the existence of an unpublished 180-word vocabulary taken by Tindale at Diamantina in 1934.
location_info: Yandama and Callabonna creeks; east to Milpa-rinka and Naryilco; at Lake Pinaroo, Tilcha, and Yandama (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Giabal is the language of the Giabal people of Toowoomba, QLD. There is little information about the meaning of the name Giabal, however it is documented throughout historical sources in addition to the names Dippil and Paiamba (Ridley 1875; Mathews 1898). The name Gomainggura, also associated with Giabal, may have the meaning 'men of the Condamine' (Tindale 1974:168).

Giabal has undergone some community-led language revitalisation. In 2013 a Giabal language wordlist was created as a part of the Condamine Alliance Languages Project (SLQ 2025).

The classification of Giabal is debated. It may be a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family. It is a potential member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:6; Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:334-5) and may be associated with the following Wakka Wakka E28 languages in addition to the Jinibara (see Dalla E25) group: Wuli Wuli E89 and Barunggam D40 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4). Giabal may also be a Turubulic (see Turrbal E86) language (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:334-5). Giabal has also been described as a variety of Bundjalung E12 (O'Grady et. al. 1966:49).

Giabal is one of the groups RH Mathews (1898:328-331) describes as the Dippil Nation, alongside Gubbi Gubbi E29, Turrbal E86, Yuggera E23, Barunggam D40, Muringam D56 and other Turubulic (see Turrbal E86) and Waka-Kabi languages (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:334-5). The Dippil Nation extends from Port Curtis in the north, south along the coast to Brisbane and the Upper Clarence region and inland including the Brisbane, Mary, Burnett, Dawson and Upper Condamine Rivers (Mathews 1898:335). Moreton and Stradbroke Islands and K'gari are also a part of the Dippil Nation.
location_info:
Giabal is located in the Darling Downs region, QLD. It extends from Ipswich in the east, south to Allora, west to Millmerran, north to Dalby and east to Toowoomba and Gatton (Capell 1963:6; Kite & Wurm 2004:6).

Neighbouring languages include Jarowair E81, Garumngar E88 and Wakka Wakka E28 to the north, Yuggera E23 and Turrbal E86 to the east and south, and Bigambul D34 to the west.

overview:
Yinhawangka is a Pama Nyungan language from Western Australia.

There is some confusion between Yinhawangka and Ngarla A48. The code A48 was originally assigned to Ngalawonga, which later became Yinhawangka as it was thought to be an alternative (and preferred) name for the same language. An additional code, A79, was created when it became apparent that the two are likely distinct language varieties, but this was originally applied to Ngalawonga (now Ngarla). The two codes have now been reversed to reflect the original assignment. As a consequence material labelled as Ngarla A48 may in fact be Yinhawangka A79. 

Von Brandenstein spoke to people in Onslow, who told him that Ini-warngga (or Ina-warngga) (A79) is the same as Niinanu, noting 'nina- is the Ina-warngga word for "to see" '. This name is associated with country south of the Pandjima and east of the Tjururu, implying this country is identified as Inawarngga [?] on Radcliffe-Brown's map1912  and Tindale's map of 1940 (1968:3). He notes that Ina-warngga spoken at Onslow was infulenced by Pandjima. 

Oates (1975:76) lists Ninaanu as an alternative name of Inawanga (A79) following von Brandenstein. Therefore, Tindale's Ninanu is listed under Yinhawangka.

Jones and Denniss report that, although Yinhawangka has been classified within the Wati subgroup by O'Grady, Voegelin and Voegelin, the variety of Yinhawangka described in the Wangka Maya 2008 publication is very similar to Banyjima A53 which is part of the Ngayarda subgroup (Wangka Maya PALC 2008:iii).
location_info:
On Hardey River south of Rocklea; southeast along upper Ashburton River from Turee Creek upstream to Kunderong Range and Angelo River; south only a short distance from the main Ashburton River channel to the north of Mount Vernon Station (Tindale 1974).

On Lyons and North Lyons rivers west to near Mount Phillips and to Peedawarra Bluff; east to eastern end of Teano Range; south to about Mount Augustus (Tindale 1974 for Ninanu).

... in the inland Ashburton region on the upper plateau of the Hamersley Ranges. Nowadays traditional country includes low-lying areas from Palm Springs, to Bellary Springs and on to Paraburdoo, including sites near Seven Mile Creek and the Ashburton River. (Wangka Maya PALC 2008:iv).

Contemporary location: Onslow, Bellary Springs community, Warrkuthurni community. (Wangka Maya PALC 2008:iv). Tom Price, Ballary Springs, Port Hedland, Woodstock (Dixon 2011:44).

overview:
Malngin ('hooked spear') is a Pama-Nyungan language of the Ngumbin sub-group; it is a dialect of Gurindji C20 (see also Eastern Gurindji C30). Nominal cases, verb conjugations and derivational processes are marked by suffixation in Malgnin; pre-verbs distinguish wider meanings for verbs. Malgin has an avoidance speech style between mother and son-in-law (Ise, 1999:3-13).

Malngin was previously listed as two separate AustLang codes: Malngin K30 and Manu C24.
location_info: Eastward limit: General limit was the drainage of Stirling Creek. Limbunya homestead was affiliated with Malngin. Midnight Yard was the easternmost extension of Malngin affiliations. Northward limit: There was no precise information on the northward limit in 2007. Bamboo Spring was affiliated with Malngin. The headwaters of the West Baines above Waterloo homestead. Waterloo homestead was affiliated with Nyiwanawu. Westward limit: There was no precise information on the westward limit in 2007. Spring Creek homestead, Mistake Creek homestead, New and Old Ord River homesteads were all affiliated with Malngin. The Bungle Bungle Range was affiliated with Gija. Southward limit: This is inferred on the basis of information Tsunoda provides on Djaru, and on the information for the northern limit of Wanyjirra (Harvey ASEDA 802).

overview:
Jarowair is the language of the Jarowair People of the Darling Downs region, QLD. The name Jarowair is believed to mean 'to give' or 'the giver' (French 1989:14).

The Jarowair People are associated with the Bunya Mountains, along with Wakka Wakka E28 and Barunggam D40. They are known for historically hosting the Bunya Nut Festival, a significant cultural event bringing together a large number of cultural groups (Ross 2008). Today, this event is being revived and celebrated by communities (Ngarrngga 2023).

Jarowair is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. In 2013 a Jarowair language wordlist was created as a part of the Condamine Alliance Languages Project (SLQ 2025). Other initiatives include cultural and language programs in preschools and schools in the area.

The classification of Jarowair is uncertain. It may be a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a potential member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:4). Jarowair may be associated with the following Wakka Wakka E28 languages in addition to the Jinibara (see Dalla E25) group: Wuli Wuli E89, Barunggam D40 and Giabal D41 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4; French 2009:1).
location_info:
Jarowair is located in the Darling Downs region, QLD. It extends north of Toowoomba and Oakey on the Rosalie Plains to Crows Nest, northwest to Bell, south to Dalby and along the western slopes of the Great Dividing Range (Tindale 1974:170; French 1989:13; Kite & Wurm 2004:6).

Neighbouring languages include Wakka Wakka E28 to the north and east, Giabal D41 to the south and Barunggam D40 to the west.

overview: Narangga is a member of the Thura-Yura L63 sub-group of Pama-Nyungan. Other members include Kaurna L3; Ngadjuri L5; Nukunu L4; Barngala L6; Adnyamathanha L10; Kuyani L9; Nauo L2 and Wirangu C1, which exhibits some differences with the Thura-Yura languages. One particular cultural-linguistic feature uniquely Thura-Yura is the use of ten birth-order names. Another are the regular pronoun forms unique to the sub-group (Simpson & Hercus 2004:179).
location_info: Yorke Peninsula; north to Port Broughton; east to Hummock Range; at Bute, Wallaroo, Ardrossan, Marion Bay, and Cape Spencer. Four named hordes are known (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Rigsby (2005 p.c.) says there appear to be two languages that go by the name Ayapathu: Ayapathu Y60 and Western Ayapathu. Western Ayapathu only recently became known; it is closely related to Ayapakanh Y64.

Verstraete and Rigsby (2015:2) report the location of (Western) Ayapathu (Y181) as being to the south-west of Yintyingka Y236. They provide grammatical information and lexical items base on a wordlist by Hamilton (//www.oocities.org/athens/delphi/2970/ayapathu.htm>, viewed 10/12/2015) as well a 1997 manuscript entitled Ayapathu fieldnotes (neither of which is in the AIATSIS collection).

Duungidjawu is the language of the Duungidjawu / Dungidau and Jinibara People of the Kilcoy area, QLD. It is a language of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup and a part of the Jinibara (see Dalla E25) people group. The name Duungidjawu is formed from the words dungi 'river' and dau 'water gum' (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).

Some language learning resources have been developed for Jinibara (see SEQILC 2025).

Wakka Wakka E28, which is related to Duungidjawu, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language programs have been implemented, including workshops and the development of language learning resources (see SEQILC 2025, Yumi Sabe 2025). Wakka Wakka E28 language programs have run across kindergarten, primary and secondary schools in and around Cherbourg, Murgon and Eidsvold, QLD.

Duungidjawu is a member of the Dalla E25 or Jinibara group. Jinibara means 'people of the lawyer cane' and comes from the word jini meaning 'lawyer cane' and the suffix -bara meaning 'people of' (Kite & Wurm 2004:4). The members of the Jinibara group differ across sources. Jinibara People Aboriginal Coorporation (2025) describe four Jinibara peoples: Dalla E25, Duungidjawu, Ngoera / Nalbo E22 and Garumngar E88. Norman Tindale (1974:166) describes the Jinibara group as Dalla E25, Duungidjawu, Ngoera / Nalbo E22, Garumngar E88 and Dungibara E87. Linguists Suzanne Kite and Stephen Wurm (2004:4) describe the Jinibara group as Dalla E25, Duungidjawu, Ngoera / Nalbo E22 and Garumngar E88. They describe Dungibara E87 as a separate group.

Duungidjawu is a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:4) and is associated with the following Wakka Wakka E28 languages in addition to the Jinibara group: Wuli Wuli E89, Djagunda E27, Barunggam D40 and Giabal D41 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).
location_info:
Duungidjawu is located in southeast Queensland. It extends from Caboolture in the east through Gunundjin at the junction of the Stanley and Brisbane Rivers, including Durundur, Villeneuve and Woodford to Mt Kilcoy (Kite & Wurm 2004:5). It also extends west to Moore and the Brisbane River and north to the Jimna Range (Kite & Wurm 2004:5).

Neighbouring languages include Dalla E25 to the north, Ngoera / Nalbo E22 to the east, Garumngar E88 to the south and Wakka Wakka E28 to the west and northwest.

overview: Crowley describes Mpakwithi as one several Anguthimri Y20 speaking groups (1981: 147).
location_info: Refer to 'Bakwithi' (map in Crowley, 1981).

overview:
Rimanggudinhma is the name of one of the two clans associated with this language. Three languages, Mbarrumbathama Y136, Rimanggudinhma and Morrobolam Y55, form a genetic subgroup of Paman known as Lamalamic. 'This subgroup is defined by shared innovations in phonology and morphology, specifically the development of voicing contrasts in trills, the setup of verbal inflections, and a number of innovative forms in nominal morphology. Within this subgroup, Umbuygamu and Lamalama form a phonologically innovative branch, while Rumanggudinhma forms a more conservative branch' (Verstraete, 2018:1-4).

Confusingly, Sommer's sketch grammar of Rimanggudinhma is entitled Koko Warra (1999). Godman says that Koko Wara Y80 is not closely related to Rimanggudinhma; despite sharing many lexical forms with Koko Wara, its verbal paradigm resembles Guugu Yimidhirr Y82 (1993:8).

Dixon groups Kuku-Wara Y80 with Rimang-Gudinhma (Y195) in his 'Lama sub-group' (2002:xxxii). Rigsby notes that the name 'Kuku Warra / Gugu Warra' is one with shifting reference, with the sense 'strange, not intelligible' (2005:138), and applied to languages that one could not understand, the opposite to Gugu Mini Y94.

In modern times people associated with this language variety often identify as Lamalama, along with Y236: Yintyingka, Y50: Umpithamu, Y55: Morrobolam and Y136: Mbarrumbathama.
location_info: Dinner Creek and Five Mile River systems, abutting Morrabalama and Umpithamu to the north and Kuku Thaypan to the south (Sutton 2007 p.c.). The Bighurrnggudinh clan has countries to the north along the Annie River, starting at Ngawal where it has a shared 'company' interest. Their southern neighbours along the Five Mile River is the Badhorrnga clan, who spoke a variety of the same language - the latter was called Port Stewart Lamalama by Ken Hale (Rigsby 1992:356).

overview:
Capell (1940) says that Wandjira (K21) is reported by speakers 'to be very close to Njinin' K7, which Capell identifies as the southern dialect of Djäru K12.

McConvell (2006 p.c.) says Wanyjira forms a dialect chain with Gurindji C20 and Jaru K12 and, as such, it is hard to say whether it is a dialect of Gurindji or Jaru.

Chikako Senge began a PhD on Wanyjirra grammar in 2008.

Wanyjirra was previously listed as two separate AustLang codes: Wanyjirra K21 and Manu C24.
location_info:
The general associations were to the drainages into Nongra Lake and the section of Sturt Creek drainage around Inverway homestead (Harvey ASEDA 802).

The Wanyjirra language was traditionally spoken around Inverway and Birrindudu stations, Northern Territory (Tsunoda 1998) [...] However, Tsunoda's data was collected mainly in traditional Djaru territory, i.e. Halls Creek or Nicholson station, Western Australia. This is because many Wanyjirra people have moved from their traditional territory into surrounding areas. (Senge 2008:4).

overview: Ogh Angkula (Y197) is classified as belonging to the Alaya-Athima language group, a set of initial-dropping languages not closely related to others of this type in the area. Alpher describes them in regional blocs, with Ogh Angkulu in the centre near Rosser Creek. Other members of this group include Awu Alaya (Kuku Thaypan) Y84; Aghu Tharrnggala Y65; Awu Arungu / Awu Alwang / Agu Aloja Y219; Ogh Alungul Y199; Kuku Mini Y94; Ikarranggal Y198; Takalak Y125; Ogh Awarrangg Y201; Ongunyjan Y206; Kokiny Y188; Athima Y237 (2016:41-42).
location_info:
Palmer River Valley & southwards (Oates 1975:291).

... near Rosser Creek [Cape York Peninsula] (West 1965 in Alpher 2016:42).

overview:
Historical records of languages in Tasmania are sparse, resulting in the decision of the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre to develop a composite language, palawa kani ('Aborigines talking'). This language incorporates materials documented since the early colonial period with surviving spoken words, texts and songs (Mansell, 2012:14).

Crowley and Dixon (1981:402-403) compare collected vocabularies from fifteen regions. This database assigns reference names for Tasmania based on this regional list. See also Northern T1; Oyster Bay T2; North-western T3; Northern Midlands T4; South-eastern T5; Macquarie Harbour T6; Ben Lomond T7; Big River T8; Cape Portland T9; South-western T10; Robbin Island T11; Circular Head T12; Port Sorrell T13; Piper River T14 and Little Swanport T15. Language data from historical sources about all Tasmanian language varieties form the basis of palawa kani (T16).
location_info: Tasmania

overview: The name Marawa appears in Berndt (1959); Capell (1963); and Oates and Oates (1970) but there appears to be no linguistic information available. Thiberger lists it as a Western Desert language A80 name (1993: 189).

Dungibara is the language of the Dungibara people from the Upper Brisbane River region, QLD. It is a language of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup and a part of the Jinibara (see Dalla E25) people group. The name Dungibara means 'people of the river' and is formed from the words duungi 'river' and the suffix -bara 'people of' (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).

Some language learning resources have been developed for Jinibara (see SEQILC 2025).

Wakka Wakka E28, which is related to Dungibara, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language programs have been implemented, including workshops and the development of language learning resources (see SEQILC 2025, Yumi Sabe 2025). Wakka Wakka E28 language programs have run across kindergarten, primary and secondary schools in and around Cherbourg, Murgon and Eidsvold, QLD.

Dungibara may be a member of the Dalla E25 or Jinibara group. Jinibara means 'people of the lawyer cane' and comes from the word jini meaning 'lawyer cane' and the suffix -bara meaning 'people of' (Kite & Wurm 2004:4). The members of the Jinibara group differ across sources. Jinibara People Aboriginal Coorporation (2025) describe four Jinibara peoples: Dalla E25, Duungidjawu E20, Ngoera / Nalbo E22 and Garumngar E88. Anthropologist Norman Tindale (1974:166) describes the Jinibara group as Dalla E25, Duungidjawu E20, Ngoera / Nalbo E22, Garumngar E88 and Dungibara. Linguists Suzanne Kite and Stephen Wurm (2004:4) describe the Jinibara group as Dalla E25, Duungidjawu E20, Ngoera / Nalbo E22 and Garumngar E88. They describe Dungibara as a separate group.

Dungibara is a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:4) and is associated with the following Wakka Wakka E28 languages in addition to the Jinibara group: Wuli Wuli E89, Djagunda E27, Barunggam D40 and Giabal D41 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).
location_info:
Dungibara is located on the Upper Pine River and D'Auguilar Range, QLD (Tindale 1974:166). It extends north of Esk and on the western side of the Brisbane River, possibly as far north as Mt Stanley (Tindale 1974:267; Steele 1983:265).

Neighbouring languages include Buyibara E24 and Wakka Wakka E28 to the north, Duungidjawu E20 to the east, Garumngar E88 to the southeast, Giabal D41 to the south and Yiman E31 and Jarowair E81 to the west.

overview: This name appears in Berndt (1959) as well as Capell (1963) and Oates and Oates (1970). According to Mura, there appears to be a word list in Bates' collection, but this needs verification. This language name is mentioned in Thieberger in association with Western Desert language A80.
Sommer (1971-1974) collected some data, and he treats it as a dialect of Oykangand Y101 (2007 p.c.)
location_info:
... at the far northwest of the Oykangand area (that would be, I guess, most downriver on the Mitchell) (Sommer according to Alpher 2007 p.c.).

Clay Hole on the north side of the Mitchell River (Sommer 2007 p.c.).

overview:
Oates says that this is included by von Brandenstein as part of Wudjari W8, which is a Noongar W41 dialect (1975:90).

Other sources (e.g. South West Aboriginal Land and Sea Council 2010) treat it as a distinct Noongar / Nyungar W41 variety and, as Kurinj (W5) language data has been recorded by Laves (MS 2189), Goreng / Koreng is treated as a distinct language in AUSTLANG. The Noongar Boodjar Waangkiny Language Centre assigns the Koreng (W5) clan to the 'Kongal-boyal - South-eastern' dialect, noting the approximate nature of 'how the original 14 recognised Noongar Clans have been drawn into 3 main dialects'.

See also the record for Noongar / Nyungar W41 for a discussion about the relationship between Noongar / Nyungar people names and language/dialect names.

Goreng / Koreng should not be confused with Gooreng Gooreng E32 and Goeng Goeng E36, two languages from Central Queensland.
location_info: From Gairdner River to Pallinup (Salt) River; at Bremer Bay; inland to Jeramungup, Pingrup, Nampup (= Nyabing), Badgebup, and Kibbleup near Broome Hill; south to Stirling Range; at Gnowangerup and Ongerup; west to Cranbrook and Tambellup but not originally at Kojonup or Qualeup; they moved west in earliest settlement times under pressure from Wudjari (Tindale 1974).

overview: This name appears in Berndt (1959) as well as Capell (1963) and Oates and Oates (1970) but there appears to be no linguistic information available on this language; possibly a Western Desert A80 variety.

The online Yolngu Matha dictionary lists wulaki as a clan name, affiliated with djinaŋ N94.1">N94.1 language.

Wulaki (N95) is a Yolngu clan affiliated with Djinang N94.1">N94.1 language and Yirritjing moiety (Waters, 1989:249).

Coleman describes Wurlaki (N95) as a clan and a language name, from the Djinang/Wurlaki workshop at Gamardi Homeland Centre School, 1994 (AILEC 0636).

The written form of the name is difficult to reproduce in the AUSTLANG reference name and thesaurus authorities; the retroflex lateral is represented in the Yolngu Matha writing system with an underlined letter: <l> (the alveaolar lateral is ). The written form Wurlaki (N95) is used in this database to maintain this distinction. For Yolngu language groups see Yolngu Matha N230.
location_info: (Djinang)

overview: Schebeck (2001:93) says that Malarrbartjaray N98 is a Ritharr?u N104 speaking Madarrpa N111 clan, which was originally a Dhuwala N199 speaking clan. Oates (1975:317) similarly lists Malarbardjuradj under Ritharrngu N104 and as a probable Mala name. In this database, Malarbardjuradj is classified in the Ritharrngu sub-group rather than Dhuwala sub-group because of the language now spoken by clan members.
location_info: (Dhuwala)

overview:
Capell (1963) says that there is some doubt about this group. Oates and Oates (1970:30) say it is reported by Bern to be virtually extinct: one speaker may still be alive.

Bradley (2007 p.c.) suspects that Wilingura may be related to Yanyuwa because various sounds exist in the place names of Wilangarra corresponds to Yanyuwa sounds.

Tindale (1974) and Harvey (ASEDA 802) provide completely different locations for this language. This database follows Harvey, who places Wilangarra (N99) next to Yanyuwa. Tindale's location is distant from Yanyuwa and inland.
location_info:
South of Mara (Basedow 1907:32).

The drainages of Bing Bong Creek, Pine Creek, and Rosie Creek. Bing Bong homestead was associated with Yanyuwa. There is no precise information on how far inland Wilangarra affiliations extended, but Lorella Spring appears to have been in the changeover zone to Marra (Harvey AILEC 0802).

... they came down onto the coast near present day Bing Bong Station and went up north to just to the north of west of Rosie Creek mouth, (Bradley 2007 p.c.).

overview:
There are several Anguthimri speaking groups: Wimaranga, Mpakwithi, Bwinitanikwithi, Baatjana, Adumakwithi, Lwipanadjini, and Bawtjathi. Crowley describes Anguthimri spoken by the Mpakwithi Y186 group, and says that because of a lack of informants, it is not possible to check to what extent dialectal differences existed among the various Anguthimri-speaking groups (Crowley, 1981:148).

In this database among Anguthimri-speaking groups only Mpakwithi Y186 and Wimarangga Y23 groups are separately listed.
location_info: ... an area from the mouth of the Mission River, west to Duyfken Point, north to the Pennefather River, and as far as the southern and western banks of the Wenlock River between about Batavia Landing and Gibson Waterhole (Crowley 1981:149-150).

overview:
Kaurna is a member of the Thura-Yura L63 sub-group of Pama-Nyungan. Other members include Nukunu L4; Ngadjuri L5; Narangga L1; Barngala L6; Adnyamathanha L10; Kuyani L9; Nauo L2 and Wirangu C1, which exhibits some differences with the Thura-Yura languages. One particular cultural-linguistic feature uniquely Thura-Yura is the use of ten birth-order names. Another are the regular pronoun forms unique to the sub-group (Simpson & Hercus 2004:179).

Teichelmann and Schürmann produced a sketch grammar (1840), which was supplemented by additional notes by Teichelmann (1858) and Teichelmann's extensive vocabulary (1857). These and other resources have been used in the reclamation of the Kaurna language, see Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/index/
location_info: Adelaide Plain (Amery 1995) Cape Jervis to Port Wakefield along eastern shore of Gulf St. Vincent; inland to near Crystal Brook, Snowtown, Blyth, Hoyleton, Hamley Bridge, Clarendon, Gawler, and Myponga; from the east side of the Hummock Range to Red Hill where northern hordes were sometimes known as the Nantuwara. Inland the Jultiwira or stringy bark forests of the Mount Lofty Ranges marked their boundary (Tindale 1974). The Map in Amery 2000 extends to north of Crystal Brook.

overview:
Ngoera / Nalbo is the name of the Ngoera / Nalbo and Jinibara People from the headwaters of the Mary River, QLD. Ngoera / Nalbo is also used as the name of a language. There is little information available about the meaning of the name Ngoera / Nalbo, however Nalbo is described as a name used by the northern neighbours of the Ngoera / Nalbo people (Langevad 1983:27). The two main spellings are represented in the language name heading.

Ngoera / Nalbo is a member of the Dalla E25 or Jinibara group. Jinibara means 'people of the lawyer cane' and comes from the word jini meaning 'lawyer cane' and the suffix -bara meaning 'people of' (Kite & Wurm 2004:4). The members of the Jinibara group differ across sources. Jinibara People Aboriginal Coorporation (2025) describe four Jinibara peoples: Dalla E25, Duungidjawu E20, Ngoera / Nalbo and Garumngar E88. Anthropologist Norman Tindale (1974:166) describes the Jinibara group as Dalla E25, Duungidjawu E20, Ngoera / Nalbo, Garumngar E88 and Dungibara E87. Linguists Suzanne Kite and Stephen Wurm (2004:4) describe the Jinibara group as Dalla E25, Duungidjawu E20, Ngoera / Nalbo and Garumngar E88. They describe Dungibara E87 as a separate group.

Ngoera / Nalbo is a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:4) and is associated with the following Wakka Wakka E28 languages in addition to the Jinibara group: Wuli Wuli E89, Djagunda E27, Barunggam D40 and Giabal D41 (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).

Ngoera / Nalbo was previously listed as two separate AustLang codes: Ngoera E90 and Nalbo E22.
location_info:
Ngoera / Nalbo is located on the Mary River plains, QLD. It extends from the headwaters of the Mary and Brisbane Rivers along the eastern slopes of the Blackall Range, north to Eumundi, south to Beerwah and Caboolture, including the Glasshouse Mountains (Tindale 1974:166; Langevad 1983:27; Jones 1990:7; Kite & Wurm 2004:5).

Neighbouring languages include Gubbi Gubbi E29 to the north and east, Duungidjawu E20 to the south and Dalla E25 to the west.

overview: This name is mentioned in Hall's study on Kuuk Thaayorre Y69 (1968).
location_info: South side of Chapman R. as /Palipan/ (1968).

overview:
There is little information available on Buyibara.

Buyibara is the proposed language name of the Buyibara people of the South Burnett region, QLD. The name Buyibara means 'people of the carpet snake', formed from the word buyi meaning 'carpet snake' and the suffix -bara which means 'people of' (Steele 1984:270; Kite & Wurm 2004:4).

Wakka Wakka E28, which may be related to Buyibara, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language programs have been implemented, including workshops and the development of language learning resources (see SEQILC 2025, Yumi Sabe 2025). Wakka Wakka E28 language programs have run across kindergarten, primary and secondary schools in and around Cherbourg, Murgon and Eidsvold, QLD.

The classification of Buyibara is uncertain. It may be a Waka-Kabi language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a potential member of the Wakka Wakka E28 subgroup (Kite & Wurm 2004:4).

Buyibara has been used as an alternative name for Ngoera / Nalbo E22. Resources on Ngoera / Nalbo E22 may be relevant.
location_info:
Buyibara is located in the South Burnett region, QLD, on Wakka Wakka E28 Country (Steele 1984:270). It extends from Kingaroy in the north, southeast to Esk and west along Blackbutt Range and the Bunya Mountains (Capell 1963:4; Steele 1984:270; Jones 2009:10).

Neigbouring languages include Wakka Wakka E28 to the north and east, Dungibara E87, Jarowair E81 and Yiman E31 to the south and Djagunda E27 to the west.

overview: Aboriginal English is one of several varieties of English spoken in Australia. It has slight regional variations including words from local traditional languages, and shares many grammatical features with other non-standard varieties in Australia.  Aboriginal English is gaining acceptance as a fully functional variety of English, along with the many other regional and social varieties of English spoken around the world.
location_info: Varieties of Aboriginal English are spoken throughout Australia.

overview:
Guwar is the language of the Ngugi and Quandamooka People of Moorgumpin (Moreton Island), QLD. Ngugi people, Goenpul people E19 and Noonuccal people E21 are together known as the Quandamooka People of Moreton Bay. The name Guwar derives from the word for 'no' (Curr 1886:229, Oates & Oates 1970:154).

Guwar is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. A number of language guides and dictionaries have been published in Guwar.

There is a strong shared culture between all Quandamooka People, who are driving the community-led language revitalisation of Jandai E19. The Jandai Language Dictionary was published by the Minjerribah Moorgumpin Elders-in-Council Aboriginal Corporation in 2011. This corporation represents the culture and language of the Goenpul people E19, Ngugi people E26 and Noonuccal people E21 of Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island) and Moorgumpin (Moreton Island). Language learning efforts have also occurred in primary schools within the Redland City Council. Jandai E19 language learning efforts have also occurred in primary schools within the Redland City Council.

Guwar is a Turubulic language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023:lxxxiv). Other Turubulic languages include Moondjan E21, Turrbal E86, Yuggera E23, Yugarabul E66, and Jandai E1.

Linguist Tony Jeffries argues that Guwar is a detached Bundjalung E12 language, and not part of the Turubulic group (Jeffries 2011). However, the classification of Guwar as a Turubulic language is more widely accepted.
location_info:
Guwar is located on Moreton Island, QLD.

Neighbouring languages include Moondjan E21 and Jandai E19 on Stradbroke Island to the south, and Yuggera E23 and Turrbal E86 on the mainland to the west.

overview:
The classification of Yirandali is uncertain. In Sutton (1973:44-45), Yirandhali (L42) is excluded from the Mari group since it shares less than 50 per cent vocabulary with its closest Maric neighbours.

Terrill (1998:99), however, tentatively includes it, cautioning that it would be premature to rule out a genetic relationship between Yirandhali and the other Maric languages.

Pooroga, Dalleburra and Yirandali (and variants) have all been used to refer to this language.

Oates (1975) says Dalleburra is a group name.

Tindale (1974) says Pooroga is the language name of the Jirandali people.

Bennett (1927) uses Dalleburra as both people and language name. Both Terrill (1998) and Sutton (1973) use Yirandhali (L42).

Curr (1886, vol. 2, pp. 460-463) gives two 'specimens' of language data for Pooroga, which he says were 'obtained probably from persons of distinct tribes'.
location_info: On upper Dutton and Flinders rivers west of the Great Dividing Range, from near Mount Sturgeon south to Caledonia; west to near Richmond, Corfield, and east of Winton; on Torrens, Tower Hill, and Landsborough Creeks; at Lammermoor, Hughenden, and Tangorin (Tindale 1974).

overview: This group is included in Crowley's description of Uradhi Y184 (1983:310). Documentation on Uradhi Y184 and its dialects may be relevant.
location_info: Between White Sands and Escape River along the Coral Sea coast was the original home of the Yadhaykenu and the Yaraytyana. The Yarattyana apparently occupied the coastal area to the north of Orford Bay. Ray's placement of Yaraytyana on his map around Bamaga (1907) is quite mistaken. Very early in the history of white settlement of the peninsula, the Yaraytyana and Yadhaykenu migrated to the Somerset area as the original Cape people became extinct (Crowley 1983:310-311).

overview: It appears that this is one of the languages related to Yuyu S19, or another name for Yuyu S19. See Clark (2005:22).
location_info: Principally on southern bank of Murray River from above Paringa, to near Mildura, Vic.; southern limits approximately 50 miles (80 km.) from river; at Ned Corner, Vic., and Salt Creek, N.S.W. (Tindale 1974). ... the country on both sides of the Murray River, below Salt Creek about Ned's Corner Station (Radcliffe-Brown 1918:247).

overview:
According to Patz (1982), this is a dialect of Kuku Yalanji Y78. Documentation on Kuku Yalanji may be relevant.

Wakaman is not to be confused with Wagaman Y108, which is an alternative name of Agwamin Y132. Previously, Wagaman was listed as a distinct language in the Language Thesaurus (Wagaman / Wakamin language (Y108)), but it is now treated as an alternative name for Agwamin Y132. Items in MURA described as relating to Wakaman (Y108) have been reassigned the appropriate heading - Wagaman Y233 or Agwamin Y132. In some cases the correct identity is not certain (Patz (2002:5) - citing Dixon and Sutton - notes that 'the name Wakaman was used by different informants for different languages'). In such case both headings have been applied.
location_info: Speakers of the Kuku Yalanji language traditionally inhabited an area of over 2000 sq km extending from the Mossman River in the south to the Annan River in the north, bordered by the Pacific Ocean in the east and extending inland to presumably just west of Mt Mulgrave (Patz 2002:6)

overview:
Gubbi Gubbi is the language of the Kabi Kabi Peoples of southeast Queensland. The name Gubbi Gubbi follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, gubbi means 'no'. This distinguishes Gubbi Gubbi from similar neighbouring languages.

Gubbi Gubbi is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. A Dictionary of the Gubbi-Gubbi and Butchulla Languages (Bell 1994) has been published. Children's picture books have also been published featuring Gubbi Gubbi language. Language learning resources, as well as school programs, have been established through community organisations. Other teaching programs and resources have been supported by the University of the Sunshine Coast and the South East Queensland Language Centre. Resources for Butchulla E30, which is a close variety of Gubbi Gubbi (Holmer 1983:138; Bell 1994), have also been created.

Gubbi Gubbi is a language of the Waka-Kabic group, a subgroup of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023:lxxxiv). It has also been grouped with Goeng Goeng E36, Gooreng Gooreng E32, and Butchulla E30 by linguist Nils Holmer (Holmer 1983:1). Gubbi Gubbi is also connected to the Jinibara group (see Dalla E25), and Taribelang E33 (O'Grady et. al. 1966:50; Wurm 1972:140).

Gubbi Gubbi are one of the groups RH Mathews (1898:328-331) describes as the Dippil Nation, alongside Giabal D41, Turrbal E86, Yuggera E23, Barunggam D40, Muringam D56 and other Turubulic and Waka Kabi languages (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:334-5). The Dippil Nation extends from Port Curtis in the north, south along the coast to Brisbane and the Upper Clarence region and inland including the Brisbane, Mary, Burnett, Dawson and Upper Condamine Rivers (Mathews 1898:335). Moreton and Stradbroke Islands and K'gari are also a part of the Dippil Nation.

Dippil has been used as an alternate name for Gubbi Gubbi and Butchulla E30. Please note that sources relating to Dippil may refer to Gubbi Gubbi.
location_info:
Gubbi Gubbi is located in southeast Queensland. It extends southwards from Bundaberg and the Burnett District along the coast, including Hervey Bay and Wide Bay, ending around the Sunshine Coast and Nambour (Mathew 1880:312; Capell 1963:6; Tindale 1974:172; Holmer 1983:2). The westernmost points are Kilkivan and Childers (Capell 1963:6). This area includes Gympie, Maryborough, and Miva.

Neighbouring languages include Gooreng Gooreng E32, Goeng Goeng E36, and Taribelang E33 to the north, Butchulla E30 on K'Gari and the adjacent mainland in the east, Dalla E25 and Ngoera / Nalbo E22 to the south, and Wakka Wakka E28 to the west and southwest.

overview: This is a dialect of Arabana L13 (Hercus,1994:6). Documentation on Arabana L13 may be relevant.
location_info: the Stuart Range and adjacent tablelands area (Hercus 1994: 6)

overview:
Northern Dharawal is the language of the Gweagal and South Coast People of Botany Bay, NSW. It is a variety of Dharawal S59. The name Gweagal can also be used to refer to the Northern Dharawal language variety.

The meaning of the name Dharawal S59 is described differently across sources. It is described as coming from the word for 'cabbage tree' (Dharawal Words 2025), but this is not consistent in the D'harawal Dreaming Stories dictionary (Andrews et. al. 2017). Arthur Capell (1956:84) describes it as meaning 'the people who say dhara for language', which is consistent with other Yuin S67 languages where the ending -wal means 'person from'. However, dhara actually means 'thigh' in Dharawal S59 (Eades 1976:74).

The name Gweagal could come from guya-gal, meaning 'south-belong', referring to the group from the south of the Kurnell Peninsula. It could also come from the name for Botany Bay, Kamay or Gamay, or the local name for La Perouse, Guriwal (Besold 2012:70). The Gujaga Foundation and present-day Dharawal S59 people residing in the south Sydney area consider Gweagal a clan or family group, and identify as speaking Dharawal S59 (Besold 2012:70; Gujaga Foundation).

Dharawal S59, which is related to Northern Dharawal, is currently undergoing language revitalisation. The Gujaga Foundation, from south Sydney, promotes language teaching and revitalisation through school programs and the publication of language learning materials. Various dictionaries and grammars have also been published.

Northern Dharawal is a Yuin-Kuri language of the Pama Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023:lxxxvi). It is a variety of Dharawal S59 along with Southern Dharawal D63, and is a member of the Yuin S67 subgroup. It is one of the northern coastal varieties of the Yuin S67 languages, along with Dharamba S56, Dyirringañ S51, and Dhurga S53 (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:102; Besold 2012:3).

The linguistic classification of Northern Dharawal as a Dharawal S59 variety is debated. Northern Dharawal (Gweagal) is considered a variety of Dharawal S59 by Arthur Capell (1970:25-6), based on vocabularies by Reverend William Ridley (1875:99-101). However, because evidence for a distinct Northern Dharawal variety is based on a short wordlist and sentences in Ridley (1875), some scholars such as Dianne Eades (1976) consider this wordlist to be Dharawal S59, and not represent an additional variety.

Languages on the NSW South Coast have been described as existing on a 'language continuum', with shared vocabulary and less defined linguistic boundaries (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:105; Besold 2012:69). For example, Dharawal S59 spoken in Botany Bay shares words with Sydney languages, but the Dharawal S59 spoken near Nowra shares words with Dharamba S56 and Dhurga S53.

The name Gweagal should not be confused with Geawegal E1, a language from the Hunter region, NSW. Some resources that refer to Gweagal may actually refer to Geawegal E1 (Wafer & Lissarague 2008:109, 165-66).
location_info:
Northern Dharawal is located in an area around the south of Botany Bay and the La Perouse area in Sydney, NSW. This includes the Kurnell Peninsula and possibly at the Georges River (Oates 1975:199). It may have extended across the majority of the Cronulla area and Sutherland Shire, west to Liverpool (Lawrence 1999:2).

Neighbouring languages include Eora S61 and Dharug / Darug S64 to the north, Dhurga S53 to the south and Gundungurra / Gandangara S60 to the west.

overview: Breen's informant identifies Minkabari as a distinct language in the same area as Pitjara L43 (Breen 1971:12). Expressing doubt about its 'dialect' status, Breen groups Minkabari with Galali D30, (Curr's) Wangkumara L25 and Pitjara L43 as the Bullo River Language (1971:27). On the other hand, Tindale lists Minkabari as the name of the language spoken by the Bitjara L43 people, while Oates (1975) says that the only information available is Wurm's assigning it as a dialect of Maljangaba L8.
location_info: At Bulloo Downs (Oates 1975:177).

overview: McDonald (2002) lists this as a people name and dialect of Ngarrindjeri. Documentation on Ngarrindjeri S69 may be relevant.
location_info: North and west of Lake Alexandrina from Grote Hill to Currency Creek; also on eastern and western extremities of Hindmarsh Island (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Dharamba is the language of the Wandandian S55, Jerrinja and South Coast Peoples of the South Coast, NSW (Tindale 1974:199-200; Jerrinja Local Aboriginal Land Council 2025). There is little information on the meaning of the name Dharamba.

Dhurga S53, which is likely related to Dharamba S56, is currently undergoing language revitalisation, with programs beginning development in the early 21st century using archival materials (Besold 2012:iii). Dhurga S53 is now being taught in local schools, such as Moruya Public School and Vincentia High School, as well as in TAFE at Moruya. A dictionary and grammar (Ellis et. al. 2020), an alphabet book (Brook 2022), and a language teaching app have been published. Language programs have also occurred within local primary schools in a reconstructed South Coast Language that uses words spoken from Bomaderry to Eden (Eden Public School 2017).

Dharamba is a Yuin-Kuri language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023:lxxxvi). It is a member of the Yuin S67 subgroup. Dharamba is one of the northern coastal varieties of the Yuin languages, along with Dharawal S59 and Dhurga S53 (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:102; Besold 2012:3).

The linguistic classification of Dharamba as a Dhurga S53 variety is still debated. Dharamba is likely a northern variety of Dhurga (Mathews 1902:58; Eades 1976:4; Besold 2012:2). However, Jutta Besold (2012:2) comments that, while Dharumba shares grammatical features with Dhurga S53, it has a more similar vocabulary to Dharawal S59.

Dharamba should not be confused with Darumbal E46, a language located in the Rockhampton and Capricorn Coast areas, QLD.
location_info:
Dharamba is located on the South Coast, NSW. It includes the localities of Braidwood, Ulladulla, Moruya, and Jervis Bay, NSW. It extends between the Shoalhaven River and Ulladulla, reaching inland to the Great Dividing Range (Besold 2012:4).

Neighbouring languages include Dharawal S59 to the north, and Dhurga S53 to the south, and Ngunawal / Ngunnawal D3 and Gundungurra / Gandangara S60 to the west.

overview:
Ngadjuri is a member of the Thura-Yura L63 sub-group of Pama-Nyungan. Other members include Kaurna L3; Nukunu L4; Narangga L1; Barngala L6; Adnyamathanha L10; Kuyani L9; Nauo L2 and Wirangu C1, which exhibits some differences with the Thura-Yura languages, influences from Western Desert languages A80. One particular cultural-linguistic feature uniquely Thura-Yura is the use of ten birth-order names. Another are the regular pronoun forms unique to the sub-group (Simpson & Hercus 2004:179).

A small picture dictionary (with accompanying CD containing sound files) was produced by Pat Waria-Read and Mary-Anne Gale with the Ngadjuri Walpa Juri Lands and Heritage Association in 2009.
location_info: From Angaston and Freeling north to Clare, Crystal Brook, Gladstone, Carrieton, and north of Waukaringa to Koonamore; east to Mannahill; in Orroroo, Peterborough, Burra, and Robertstown districts (Tindale 1974:214).

overview:
The online Yolngu Matha dictionary describes ngaymil as a clan-nation affiliated with dhangu'mi N192.

Ngaymil (N116.X">N116.X) is a Yolngu clan affiliated with Dhangu N192 language and Dhuwa moiety (Schebeck, 2001:16).

For Yolngu language groups see Yolngu Matha N230.
location_info: (Dhangu)

overview: Tindale lists Ndomdorin (Y40) under Winduwinda as a group name. However, Oates (1975:383) suggests it is 'probably a Wik language'. According to Sutton (2001:460), it seems that the origin of the term Winduwinda is fundamentally geographical, centering on the Winda Winda Creek area and covering groups with lands between the Archer and Mission Rivers.
location_info:
Aurukun Mission area, Q. (Oates & Oates 1970:199).

Eastern Cape York [SD54-03]. Traditionally spoken in Winda Winda Creek, between Archer and Mission Rivers. Following removals later spoken in the Northern Peninsula Area [SC54-15]: New Mapoon, Injinoo and Cowal Creek communities. (State Library of Queensland ).

overview:
Schebeck (2001:17) reports that Dhalwaŋu N143.1">N143.1 people have adopted Nuŋgubuyu N128 as their language and they are called Nuŋudulpuy (or possibly Nhuŋudulpuy) (N116.Y">N116.Y).

Heath (1980:3) describes Nungudulbuy (N116.Y">N116.Y) as Day'yi N118 speaking people, most of whom have been absorbed by the Nunngubuyu N128, and who are sometimes considered a sub-group of Madarpa N111.

For Yolngu languages see Yolngu Matha N230.

There is little information available on Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language.

Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language is a language of the Central Coast, NSW. It is a potential variety used by coastal Darkinyung S65 people. The name 'Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language' is used by linguists Jim Wafer and Amanda Lissarrague (2008:143) to refer to the coastal variety of Darkinyung S65 documented by Tuckerman (1887). There is no Indigenous name recorded for this variety.

Little is known about the Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language people because this name appears to reflect a research perspective rather than a community perspective. Wafer and Lissarrague (2008:143) believed that the coastal Darkinyung S65 people were associated with the Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language. Their research suggests Eora S61, Dharug / Darug S64, Darkinyung S65 and Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language are separate communities using languages with coastal and inland varieties (Wilkins & Nash 2008:485-6). This has not been confirmed elsewhere.

Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language is one of two varieties of the Hawkesbury-MacDonald River language, a Pama-Nyungan language from the north shore of the Hawkesbury River (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:143-145). The Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language is the coastal variety of the Hawkesbury-MacDonald River language, and Darkinyung S65 is the inland variety (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:143-145). It is also associated with Eora S61 and Dharug / Darug S64 (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:140).
thes_lang_head: Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language S96
location_info:
Hawkesbury River - Broken Bay language is located on the Central Coast of NSW. It extends across the north side of Broken Bay and the lower region of the Hawkesbury River (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:144). This region is also described as Darkinyung S65 Country.

Neighbouring languages include Wanarruwa S63 to the north, Awabakal S66 to the east, Dharug / Darug S64 in the south and Wiradjuri D10 to the west.

overview:
Wik-Ep (Y52) is called Wik-Iit by speakers; the clan whose estate lies between that of Wik-Ep and Wik-Me'anh Y53 is known by either of these two names, it is said to be like these two languages but different from both (Sutton, 1991:56-57).

This language belongs to a genetic language family (shared origins) which includes: Wik-Mungkan Y57; Wik-Iiyanh Y177 and Y172; Wik-Ngathan Y54 and Y56; Wik-Ngatharr Y51; Wik-Me'anh Y53; Wik-Keyangan Y173; Mungkanho; Kugu-Uwanh Y176; Kugu Muminh Y43; Kugu-Ugbanh Y175 and Kugu-Mu'inh Y53 (Sutton, 1993:32).
location_info: ... countries on the middle Kirke River (Sutton 1978:37).

overview: Dhay'yi (~Dhayi'yimirr) is a Yolngu language N230. Clans affiliated with Dhay'yi include Djarrwark N117 (Dhuwa moiety) and Dhalwangu N143.1">N143.1 (Yirritja moiety). See also Nuŋudulbuy N116.Y">N116.Y and Madarrpa N111.
location_info: Shores of Blue Mud Bay north to the Koolatong River and inland to an important source of implement stone at Ngilipidji (Tindale 1974).

overview:
The language from the region known as Hunter River and Lake Macquarie to the north of Sydney is known from the work of the Rev Lancelot Threlkeld (1788-1859) who established a mission at Lake Macquarie between 1826 - 1841.

Threlkeld studied the language under the guidance of Biraban, also known as Johnny McGill, who later worked as an interpreter in court cases involving Aboriginal people.

Threlkeld's major descriptions of the language from the Hunter River and Lake Macquarie region published in 1834 and 1850 were later rearranged, condensed and edited by Fraser, his version was published in 1892 (this edition is usually attributed to Threlkeld). It includes a new orthography (writing system) designed by Fraser, who named language 'Awabakal' S66 which has since been adopted by the community (1892:preface).

Arposio (2008:10) describes Awabakal S66 as a dialect within a larger language group including Gadhang E67 to the north and extending southwards from Newcastle down the coast to the northern shores of Botany Bay, reflecting Fraser's (1892) 'Kuringgai' group.

Lissarrague describes the Hunter River - Lake Macquarie language (S99) spoken by people now known as Awabakal S66, Kuringgai S62, Wonnarua S63 and possibly Geawegal E1 (2006:8).

In Wafer and Lissarrague, Awabakal S66 is treated as a dialect name of the Hunter River - Lake Macquarie language, the other dialects being Wanarruwa S63 and Karikal S62, the latter is also known as Kurringgai, which Wafer and Lissarrague speculate is another invention of Fraser (2008:159-160). Their paper in 2010 disambiguates the different uses of this term.

Wafer and Lissarrague (2008) also address the confusion over the relationship between the Hunter River - Lake Macquarie language (S99) (i.e. Wanarruwa 63, Karikal ~ Kuringgai S62, Kayawaykal E1) and the 'Lower North Coast language' (i.e. Gathang E67, Birrpay E3, Warrimay E2 and Guringay E95), indicating these are two distinct languages.
thes_lang_head: Hunter River - Lake Macquarie language S99
location_info: The name of the Hunter River - Lake Macquarie language describes its regional distribution. See locations listed the various dialects: Awabakal (S66), Wanarruwa (S63), Kuringgai (S62) and Kayawaykal (E1).

overview: While Watha wurrung (S29) is genetically related to 'Daung wurrung S37, Boon wurrung S35, Woi wurrung S36, Djab wurrung S26, Djadja wurrung S31.1">S31.1, and other "Kulin" dialects', it has diverged so much that it might be considered a separate language (Dixon in Clarke 1996:17).
location_info: ... from the coast around Geelong inland to include Beaufort and Ballarat (Blake 1988:59). ... south of Geelong toward Lorne, north toward Ballarat and then south east to the Werribee River (Pascoe 2003:19). ... between the Werribee River, Mt Emu, the northern shores of Lake Corangamite and Birregurra, including the coast east of Cape Otway (Scarlett 1977:2).

overview: According to Oates (1975:140), Hudson reported that Njardi (A91) is a north-west dialect of Walmadjari A66. However, it does not seem to be recognised by Hudson and Richards, who have done extensive research on Walmajarri A66. Harvey (ASEDA 802) reports that Walmajarri speakers in the 1960s associated an area with Nyardi (identified as such on Harvey's map) but nothing is recorded of this language.
location_info: Cf. map in Harvey (2008)

overview:
Pungupungu is a non-Pama Nyungan language from the Daly River region of the Northern Territory.

Tryon compiled a sketch grammar and reports that Wadyiginy N31 and Pungupungu share approximately 79% cognates and would thus be normally treated as dialects of the same language. However, there exists serious morphological or morphologico-typological differences between them (1974:187). Tryon's early classification of Daly River languages as a single family has been revised and divided into five families; Reid and Harvey include an Anson Bay family consisting of Paccamalh N31 and Pungu-Pungu (N11) (in Evans, 2003:13).

Green says the term PunguPungu is used in the modern Daly to refer to a western MalakMalak N22 dialect (2007 p.c.). See also Tindale (1974:235) who includes an ambiguous reference to Mulukmuluk N22 regarding Pungupungu.

Pungu Pungu, also called Kandjerramalh, is a dialect closely related to Batjamalh, although there are some grammatical differences (according to Tryon 1974). It is placed in the Anson Bay group of Daly languages with Batjamalh N31 (Green & Nordlinger viewed November 2020).
location_info:
... on the North bank of Daly River (Stanner 1933 as quoted by Tryon 1974). On both banks of the Daly River inland from the coastal Wogait (Tindale 1974). ... south of the Wogait, on the Daly river (Basedow 1907:2).

Traditional Pungu Pungu country was on the north bank of the Daly River, south of Batjamalh country (Green & Nordlinger, viewed November 2020).

overview:
Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi is a language of the Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi and Gomeroi People of north central New South Wales and southern Queensland. Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi community recognise multiple spellings. The three main preferred spellings are represented in the language name heading.

The name Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi follows the 'no'-'having' structure of many neighbouring language names, with gamil (or kamil) meaning 'no' and the suffix -araay (or -aroi) meaning 'having/to have' or 'with'. This distinguishes Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi from similar neighbouring languages.

Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Community-developed and led language programs were adopted by schools in Walgett, Toomelah-Boggabilla, Goodooga and Lightning Ridge in the mid to late 1990s (Giacon 2017:v). A Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi language course began to be taught at TAFE NSW in 1995, and then periodically at the University of Sydney and at the Australian National University from 2006. In 2025, Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi was also being taught at schools in Coonabarabran, Tamworth, Gunnedah, Moree, Inverell and Qurindi.

Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi is closely associated with Yuwaalaraay D27 and Yuwaalayaay D54, which are situated west of Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi Country. Although these languages share a substantial number of words and have similar grammars, they are considered different languages by communities (Giacon 2017:2). Nevertheless, many learning resources cater to all three languages, such as the Gamilaraay/Yuwaalaraay/Yuwaalayaay Dictionary (Ash et. al. 2003).

Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi is a Central-NSW language within the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023:lxxxiv). It has a number of varieties including: Guyinbaraay D15, Wirraay-Wirraay D66, Yuwaalraay D27, Yuwaalayaay D54, Wiriyaraay D28, and Gawambaraay D39 (Ash, Giacon & Lissarrague 2003:2-3). These are sometimes grouped together and referred to as the Darling Tributaries language (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:215).
location_info:
Gamilaraay/Gamilaroi/Kamilaroi is located in northwest New South Wales. It is roughly bounded by Walgett, Goodooga, Mungindi, Goondiwindi, Ashford, Tamworth, Murrurundi and Coonabarabran (Ash, Giacon & Lissarrague 2003:5).

Peter Austin (2008:38) describes the Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi region as a little broader, saying that it was spread 'over a vast area of New South Wales [...extending] west of the Great Dividing Range, apparently from as far south as near the current town of Murrurundi and the Page River, to the areas where are now located Tamworth, Narrabri, Moree, Boggabilla, Mugindi, Collarenebri, Walgett and Gunnedah.'

Neighbouring languages include Yuwaalaraay D27 and Yuwaalayaay D54 to the west, Bigambul D34 to the north, Wayilwan D20 and Wiradjuri D10 to the south, and Bundjalung E12, Ngarbal E68, Gumbayngirr E7, Southern Anaiwan D24, Birrbay E3, and Gweagal E1 to the east.

overview:
According to Blake (1991:31), this is a dialect of the same language as Boonwurrung S35 and Thagungwurrung S37.

Blake says the language has no name but he refers it as Woiwurrung (thus using Woiwurrung as both dialect and language name), he also calls it 'the Melbourne language'. He refers to the people who spoke these dialects as Kulin, noting that this is a narrower use of the term than is usual.

Blake (1991:30, 49) also indicates a possible additional dialect in the northern Thagungwurrung area, Ngoorra S83, which he says takes its name from the Ngoora-yilam clan. Blake reports that this dialect is identified by Barwick (1984:125), but says it may simply have been an alternative name for Thagungwurrung.

Clan names associated with Woiwurrung include Wurundjeri-balluk, Buluk-wilam, Kunnung-willam-baluk, Talam-willam, Kurung-jang-baluk, Marin-bulluk or Boi-berrit, Kurnaje-berreing (Blake: 1991: 46-47).

Oates (1975:189) subsumes S36 (Woiwurung in Oates and Oates 1970) under S37 (Daungwurung in Oates and Oates 1970), and assigns Woiwurung as a standard name for S37.
location_info:
Yarra Valley from the catchment area down to Heidelberg (Wurundjeri-balluk tribe), south of the Yarra valley extending down to Dandenong, Cranbourne and the Koo-wee-rup Swamp (Buluk-wilam tribe), between Mount Macedon and Daylesford (Kunnung-willam baluk tribe), around Bacchus Marsh (Kurung-jang-baluk tribe), land to the west of the Maribyrnong with Sunbury as a centre (Marinbulluk or Boi-berrit tribe), between Maribyrnong and the Yarra (Kurnaje-berreing tribe) (Blake 1991:46-47).

Yarra and Maribynong watersheds, bounded on the north by the Dividing Range from Mt. Bawbaw westward to Mt. William and Mt. Macedon, and on west by the Werribee River, defined by Robinson and Howitt's Kulin informants as the boundary between Woi wurrung and Wada wurrung (Clark 1990:379).

overview:
Wirraay-Wirraay is a proposed language from the Balonne River area of southern Queensland. It may be the language referred to by D57 Weraerai or D28 Wiriyaraay. The name Wirriwirri (Wiriwiri) may also refer to Wirraay-Wirraay (Wafter & Lissarrague 2008:219).

Wirraay-Wirraay follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, wirraay means 'no'. This distinguishes Wirraay-Wirraay from similar neighbouring languages.

Wirraay-Wirraay is a central-inland NSW language within the Pama-Nyungan language family (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:215). Similar languages include: Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23, Yuwaalraay D27, Yuwaalayaay D54, Wiriyaraay D28, Guyinbaraay D15, and Gawambaraay D39 (Ash, Giacon & Lissarrague 2003:2-3). These are sometimes grouped together and referred to as the Darling Tributaries language (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:215). Wirraay-Wirraay is described as a language distinct from Wiriyaraay D28 and Wirraayaraay D65 (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:219).
location_info: Wirraay-Wirraay is located around the Balonne River in South-Central Queensland, near the New South Wales border (Barlow 1873:174 in Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:219).

overview:
This is one of the Woi wurrung S36 clans (Clark, 1990:383).

Tindale considers this to be a Wathaurung S29 group and says their language is called Jibberin. Jibberin appears to come from a word list in Curr (1887) entitled 'Moorabool-Jibberin language', but Oates (1975:411) identifies it as a Jarra S31.1">S31.1 word list.

Based on the information available, Kurung is unlikely to be a language name.
location_info: ... west side of Port Phillip Bay between Werribee River and Geelong; inland up Moorabool River to Dividing Range; westward toward Ballarat; at Ballan (Tindale 1974).

overview: Oates and Oates (1970:202) list this, but in her later work Oates (1975:287,383) deletes this, saying it was an informant's name. Jolly (1989:16) suspects that Juwula (Y70) is an alternative name of Aghu Tharnggala Y65.
location_info:
Juwula (Capell,1963: Y75)

Location: Headwaters of Hahn and Morehead Rivers and westwart across the Divide to headwaters of Alice R. (LMW).

Information: Studied by L. West from the last speaker.

overview:
Wirraayaraay is the name of a people group affiliated with Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23 and Gomeroi People from the area surrounding the Gwydir River and Moree, Northern New South Wales. It can also refer to a proposed variety of Wiradjuri D10.

The name Wirraayaraay may be an exonym used by speakers of Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23 following the 'no'-'having' pattern seen in many surrounding languages, where wirraay is the Wirraayarray and Wiraadjuri D10 word for 'no', and -(y)aay is a Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23 suffix meaning 'having'.

The Wirraayaraay community is associated with the area on the north side of the Gwydir River, from Moree to Bingara (Tindale 1974:200). Wirraayaraay people are historically affiliated with Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23. Reports by Reverend C.C. Greenway (1878:233-46) indicate a strong shared culture and tradition. Wirraayaraay is the preferred term used by the Friends of Myall Creek committee.

However, there is little information known about Wirraayaraay as a language, as it may refer to many other languages. It has been associated with Weraerai D57, Wiriyaraay D28, and Wirraay-Wirraay D66.

Linguists Jim Wafer and Amanda Lissarrague (2008:218-219) attempt to locate and identify Wirraayaraay more precisely by distinguishing it from Wiriyaraay D28 and Wirraay-Wirraay D66. They point to wordlists provided in the journal Science of Man (Thomas 1900:168, 1901a:26, 1901b:44; Maguire 1907a:80, 1907b:95, 1910:180) to show that Wirraayaraay is more closely related to Wiradjuri D10 than languages further north.

Weraerai D57 has been used as an alternative name for Wirraayaraay, but it has also been used to refer to Yuwaalaraay D27.
location_info: Wirraayaraay is located in an area surrounding the Gwydir River, encompassing Moree, Bingara, Warialda, Yallaroi and Wallangra (Capell 1963:17; Tindale 1974:200). Wafer and Lissarrague (2008:218) argue that it was spoken 'south of Gamilaraay', placing it closer to Dubbo, Gilgandra, and Coonabaraban, bordering Wiradjuri D10.

overview:
Green (1989) treats this as a dialect of Marrithiyel N7. There is an article by Tryon (1970).

Green and Nordlinger classify Marri Tjevin as a Western Daly non Pama-Nyungan language along with Marramaninjsji N16, Merranunggu N13, Emmi N15, Menthe N6, Marri Ngarr N102, Makati ke N163, Marrithiyel N7, Marri Ammu N162, and Marri Dan N9 (viewed November 2020).
location_info:
Swamplands at mouth of Moyle River and coastal country near Cape Dombey (Tindale 1974).

Marri Tjevin and Marri Ammu are two closely related dialects whose country lies along the coast north of the mouth of the Moyle River, extending up towards the Dashwood Plains. Marri Tjevin occupies the southern part of this area, with Magati Ke and Marri Ngarr to the south. Marri Ammu then has Menthe and Merranunggu to its north and north-east respectively. Their sister dialect Marrithiyel lies to their east. There are a number of active outstations on Marri Tjevin and Marri Ammu country proper, with Marri Tjevin and Marri Ammu communities also resident at Wadeye (Green & Nordlinger viewd November 2020).

overview:
This is a people name according to Oates and Oates (1970:202, 209).

However, West (1965) made recordings of a language he termed Araku / ?A?u- (Y75), for which he mentions 'Kuku Wara' Y80 as an alternative name. It may be that A'ragu is a dialect of Kuku Wara. Rigsby (1979:90) acknowledges that Koko Warra Y80 is little known and may refer to more than one language, as does Black (1975:1).

Given this, A'ragu is now a distinct language heading in this database, rather than an alternative name for Koko Wara (though it may be a closely related dialect).
location_info:
Between Laura and Cape Stakey, south of Princess Charlotte Bay, Q (Capell 1963, Oates & Oates 1970:202).

Laura area to Jack Lakes (West 1965).

overview:
Jones (2002:12-20) says it appears that the term Wangkajunga was introduced sometime in the early 1970s by the Western Desert people at Christmas Creek and Fitzroy Crossing as a means to identify themselves as desert people and to distinguish themselves from Walmajarri A66 and Yulparija A67. The term is now used as both the name of a particular dialect of the Western Desert language A80 and as a cover term for several of these dialects.

Wangkajunga has a complex system of pronominal clitics which cross-reference subject, object and dative arguments; also clitics for cross-referencing animate allative and ablative participants. The clitics mark the first word or consituant of the clause. The compulsory nature of this complex feature is shared with other north west varieties of Western Desert Languages A80, including Kukatja A68, Manyjilyjarra A51.1">A51.1, Yulparija A67, and Pintupi C10, distinguishing them from the southern languages Pitjantjatjara C6 and Yankunytjatjara C4. This type of clitic cluster is not as compex in Ngaanyatjarra, and is not obligatory in Yankunytjatjara (Jones, 2011:9-10).
location_info:
... north-eastern section of the Great Sandy Desert and the Canning Stock Route (Jones 2002). South and west of Lake Gregory (Oates 1975:126).

Contemporary location: Fitzroy Crossing, Christmas Creek Station, Bohemia Downs Station Fitzroy Valley (Jones 2002).

overview:
Dhudhuroa is the language of the Dhudhuroa people of the Ovens Murray region, VIC. The name Dhudhuroa follows a common pattern of many Australian language names. The first syllable of dhubalga (dhu-) meaning 'no' is repeated, with the shortened form of the suffix -wurru (-wa) meaning 'language' or 'mouth' (Blake & Reid 2002:179). The full language name would be Dhu-dhu-(wu)rru-wa (Blake & Reid 2002:179). This distinguishes Dhudhuroa from similar neighbouring languages.

Dhudhuroa traditional groups include Boengar-mittung, Djilamatang S95, Ginning-mittung, Tarrer-mittung, and Theddora-mittung (Clark 2009:219-20).

Dhudhuroa is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language projects have been undertaken in collaboration with organisations including the University of Melbourne (Indigenous Knowledge Unit 2024), Victorian Aboriginal Corporation for Languages (VACL 2026), First Languages Australia (FLA 2026), and the Language Data Commons of Australia (2026). Language resources have been developed and Dhudhuroa has been taught in schools across northeastern Victoria (Dhudhuroa Teaching & Learning 2024).

Dhudhuroa shares connections with Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 and Gundungerre / Yaithmathang S43. Dhudhuroa and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 have collaborated on language revitalisation work (Eira 2008:152). Previously, Dhudhuroa and Gundungerre / Yaithmathang S43 have been described as a part of the same language or people group (see O'Grady et. al. 1966:48; Tindale 1974:204).
