Today, they are recognised as independent communities and languages (see Eira 2008).

Dhudhuroa is a language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Eastern Victoria language group, along with Kurnai S68 and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 (Bowern 2023). It is one of two languages of the Mitta Mitta River drainage basin, the other language being Gundungerre / Yaithmathang S43 which is located further to the south (Clark 2009:219). The relationship between Dhudhuroa and neighbouring languages is uncertain, because Dhudhuroa shares only a few linguistic features with them (Blake & Reid 2002:183).
location_info:
Dhudhuroa is located in the Ovens Murray region, VIC. It extends on the Victorian side of the Murray River, from Albury in the east to Jingellic and Tintaldra in the west (Tindale 1974:204; Blake 1998:3; Eira 2008:152). This area includes the Mitta Mitta and Kiewa rivers.

Neighbouring languages include Wiradjuri D10 to the north, Walgalu S47 to the east, Gundungerre / Yaithmathang S43 and Kurnai S68 to the south, and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 to the west.

overview:
According to Oates (1975:376), the only information available is Tindale's mapping, but Tindale (1974) does provide some references. Tindale cites Williams' word list in Curr (1886) but Oates identifies this source as Ngadjunma A3 data, while MURA identifies it as Mirning A9.

Thieberger mentions this name associated with Western Desert language A80.
location_info: Northern margin of Nullarbor Plain from Naretha to about north of Loongana; northward for about 100 miles (160 km.); at Rawlinna and Walawuluna Rockhole (Tindale 1974).

overview: Oates (1975:293, 383) says that this is an alternate name of Gugu Bera Y85, while Tindale (1974) says that it is a name used by neighbouring language groups for Kokopera Y85. See and use  Y85: Koko Bera
location_info: ... coast south of Nassau River, Q (Oates & Oates 1970:203).

overview:
According to Oates (1975:139) both Hudson and Richards reported on this dialect. However, Hudson and Richards (2008 p.c.) say they never confirmed the existence of this dialect and they have not been using this term. They suspect that the name Nyanyany could be a variant of Nyininy K7.

Kolig (nd: 2) reports Njanjan (A90) as one of three dialects of Wolmadjeri A66. He locates it 'between the south-east of Bohemia Downs and Sturt Creek, with the southernmost point Gregory Salt Lake (Barugu)' and describes it as 'heavy or half Wolmadjeri'.
location_info: ... between the south-east of Bohemia Downs and Sturt Creek, with the southernmost point Gregory Salt Lake (Barugu) (Kolig, nd: 2)

overview:
There is little information available on Karunbara.

Karunbara is the language of the Karunbara / Warabal and Darumbal People of Yeppoon, QLD. It is a variety of Darumbal E46. There is little information about the meaning of the name Karunbara.

Warabal (Karunbara) is one of four people groups who are associated with the mainland varieties of Darumbal E46. The other people groups are Nindybul, Tarumbul (Darumbal) and Kuinmabra (Guwinmal E49)(Terrill 2002:13; Darumbal People Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC 2025).

Darumbal E46, which is related to Karunbara, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. In 2002 a reference grammar Dharumbal: The language of Rockhampton, Australia was created by Darumbal-Noolar Murree Aboriginal Corporation for Land and Culture and linguist Angela Terrill. Cultural and language education programs have run on Darumbal Country (Darumbal People Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC 2025).

Karunbara is a mainland variety of Darumbal E46, a language of the Pama-Nyungan language family. The other mainland Darumbal E46 varieties are Guwinmal E49 and Rakiwara E83. Wapabara E82 is a variety on the islands of Keppel Bay.

The classification of Darumbal E46 is debated. Recently, Darumbal E46 was described as a Greater Maric language of the Dharambalic family (Bowern 2023). It has also been described as a Waka-Kabi language (see Wakka Wakka E28 and Gubbi Gubbi E29)(O'Grady et. al. 1966:50; Wurm 1972:140). However, Darumbal's E46 relationship to neighbouring languages is uncertain (Holmer 1983:456; Terrill 2002:15).
location_info:
Karunbara is located in Rosewood, Central Queensland, on Darumbal E46 Country (Tindale 1974:21). Karunbara people are described as traditionally travelling to Morinish, Yaamba, Westwood, Rockhampton and along the Dawson River to Duaringa (Roth 1898 in Terrill 2002:13).

Neighbouring languages include Biri E56 varieties to the north and west, and Baiali E42 to the south.

overview:
Pindiini, Wangkatja A103 and Wangkatha A12 are listed as separate dialects of the Western Desert language A80 in this database but they appear to be very close to each other and hardly distinguishable. Pindiini may be an alternative name of Wangkatja A103 or Wangkatha A12.

However, on the basis of the distinct location given by Tindale (1974), it is treated as a separate dialect; Tindale lists Wanggada as an alternative name of Pindiini. Between Pindiini and Wangkatha/Wangkatja, Tindale's map shows two other groups, Murunitja A8 and Tjeraridjal A7.

The ABS treats Pindiini and Wangkatja as alternative names of Wangkatha so census information on Wangkatha may be relevant to Pindiini and Wangkatja. Documentation on Wangkatha A12 may be relevant.
location_info: Northern margin of Nullarbor Plain from north of Hughes, So. Aust., to north of Loongana; northward from the plain margin for about 150 miles (240 km.) (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Dixon (2002, 2007 p.c.) treats Thaagurda as a possible name for Cheangwa language on the basis of the location of Thaagurda W15 given in Marmion (1996).

Blevins (2001:5) suspects that Cheangwa is a Nhanda W14 word - 'Jianga' is the name of a place near the Murchison where there is a big thicket and '-waa' is the Nhanda suffix meaning 'with'.

O'Grady et al. treat Cheangwa as an alternative name for Widi A13.

Thieberger (1993) lists Cheangwa as an alternative name for Wajarri A39.

Language data from Perks in Curr (1886) is associated with the name Cheangwa, though the name is used only to describe the location of a 'tribe' and their language, neither of which are named. This location is within the boundaries described for both Widi A13 and Daguda W15. A comparison of the data in Curr with other language data may clarify the identity of 'Cheangwa'. Until more is known, Cheangwa is treated as a distinct language variety.
location_info: Cheangwa Hill' (Coordinates: 116.23 x 27.29).

overview:
Singer et al. (2021:1) say that Ilgar (N184) is a non-Pama Nyungan language in the Iwaidjan language family, the others in this family are Iwaidja N39, Mawng N64, Amurdak N47, Marrku N45, Wurrugu N37 and Garig N188.

Evans classifies this in the non-Pama Nyungan Iwaidjan family. Evans (1996) contains some data about Ilgar.
location_info: Grant Island near Croker Island (Harvey PMS 5822). The islands east of Croker Island including Darch Island (Harvey AILEC 802). ... situated among the islands in the vicinity of Croker (Marrala et al. 2008:viii)

overview:
Gratte (1998) provides transcriptions of language data recorded from a speaker who called it Nowkadja (A101), though he suggests the alternative Ngukaja (A101), the spelling also used by Daisy Bates (Gratte 2007). Gratte notes that the Aboriginal community of the Geraldton (Chapman Valley) area has adopted this spelling and treat it as 'their tribal name for the Geraldton area'. He says that this is not quite accurate as there were likely about four dialects with a 100 km radius of Geraldton.

Von Brandenstein (1967:2) worked with the same speaker as Gratte but reports different names supplied by the speaker - Njaakurdi and Nanagarri - and notes that the language was clearly a mix of more than one variety, including Wadjarri A39 and Nanda W14 in addition to 'Njaakurdi'.

It is not clear whether 'Njaakurdi' is a variant of Ngukaja, but Douglas (1976:6) gives 'Nangarri' as a variant of his Noongar / Nyungar W41 dialect, Nanakati A93. Blevins (2001) conflates these two names (as does Oates 1975), describing the southern dialect of Nhanda W14 as 'Amangu W12 (also known as Amandyo, Nhaaguja (A101?), Njaagurdi, and Nyaakurti A93?'. She locates it 'from Geraldton (Champion Bay) south to Hill River and inland to Mullewa', an area which takes in the area of Nhanhagardi A93 described by Elefsiniotis (2008 p.c.).

Marmion (2007 p.c.) says that based on the wordlists available from the region, it appears Ngukaja (A101) would have been mutually intelligible with Nhanda W14. Thus, he suspects that it is a dialect of Nhanda.
location_info: Chapman Valley (Gratte, 1998)

overview:
Wapabara is the language of the Woppaburra People of the islands of Keppel Bay, QLD. It is a variety of Darumbal E46. The name Wapabara means 'people of the island'. It derives from wapa, meaning 'island' and the suffix -bara meaning 'people of' (Terrill 2002:12).

Wapabara is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Language work has been undertaken via the Priority Languages Support Project (First Languages Australia 2025).

Wapabara is a variety of Darumbal E46, a language of the Pama-Nyungan language family. It is located on the islands of Keppel Bay. The mainland varieties of Darumbal E46 are Guwinmal E49, Rakiwara E83 and Karunbara E84.

The classification of Darumbal E46 is debated. Recently, Darumbal E46 was described as a Greater Maric language of the Dharambalic family (Bowern 2023). It has also been described as a Waka-Kabi language (see Wakka Wakka E28 and Gubbi Gubbi E29)(O'Grady et. al. 1966:50; Wurm 1972:140). However, Darumbal's E46 relationship to neighbouring languages is uncertain (Holmer 1983:456; Terrill 2002:15).
location_info:
Wapabara is located on the islands of Keppel Bay, QLD. This includes the islands of Konomie (North Keppel Island), Woppa (South / Great Keppel Island) and Burye (Humpy Island)(Terrill 2002:12; Woppaburra TUMRA 2020).

Neighbouring languages on the mainland include Darumbal E46 varieties to the east and Baiali E42 to the south.

overview:
McDonald (2002:15) comments that Ngaralti (S4), Nganguruku S6, Ngaiawang S7 and Ngawait S10 seem to be closely related each other. However, she also notes that, according to Tindale (1974), vocabularies of these groups show differences.

Wafer and Lissarrague (2008:31) also group them together under the 'Lower Riverland language', though they note that the names are more likely to be dialects than 'alternative designations', citing the distinct locations and differences in kinship terms described in Radcliffe-Brown (1918:243).

Previously the Thesaurus had both Ngaralda and Brabirawilung as reference names for S4. However, according to Hercus (1965), Brabirawilung was from Gippsland, which does not correspond with the location of Ngaralda identified by Capell (1963). Further, Brabirawilung is given as an alternative of Brabralung S45 by Wurm (1972). Consequently, some of the items identified as Ngaralda in MURA may actually relate to Brabralung S45.
location_info: On Murray River from Wood Hill to Port Mannum, to Bremer Creek, Palmer, Mt. Lofty Ranges, S.A. (Oates & Oates 1970:130, Capell 1963). the banks of the Murray River between Swanport and Mannum (Radcliffe-Brown 1918:243). Murray River from Wood Hill to Port Mannum; west to Bremer Creek, Palmer, and eastern scarp of Mount Lofty Ranges (Tindale 1974).

overview:
MacPherson (1904) recognises two groups within the area described for Anewan D24 by Mathews (1903). According to MacPherson the Himberrong D69 and the Inuwon could understand each other, but not the Enneewin D64 (in Crowley (1976:22-23).

Crowley notes the uncertain identity of these names, being 'either closely related dialects ... or sub-tribal units', but uses the term Nganjaywana D24 as a cover term for the two.
location_info: West of the Range from Bundarra to Uralla. (MacPherson 1904:678)

overview:
Dharug / Darug is the language of the Dharug / Darug people of the Sydney region, NSW. It is also known as 'the Sydney language' (Troy 2019:1). Eora S61 may be a Dharug / Darug variety. Dharug / Darug community recognise multiple spellings. The two main preferred spellings are represented in the language name heading.

There is little information about the meaning of the name Dharug / Darug, however it was documented and adopted from the 1870s to refer primarily to the inland or hinterland Dharug / Darug community (Attenbrow 2010:31).

Dharug / Darug is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Community-led language resources have been developed by the Bayala Aboriginal Corporation (Bayala 2026), including a dictionary app, high school textbook and songbooks. Dharug / Darug language programs have been adopted by preschools and schools across Western Sydney (Seymour et. al. 2025:1102). In 2024 Dharug / Darug language courses ran at Macquarie University and Western Sydney University.

Dharug / Darug is a Sydney-Central Coast language (Bowern 2023) of the Pama-Nyungan language family. It is also described as an inland language of the Sydney-Hawkesbury language group, alongside the coastal language Eora S61 (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:140). Dharug / Darug is associated with Eora S61, Darkinyung S65 and Hawkesbury River-Broken Bay language S96 (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:140).

The relationship between Eora S61 and Dharug / Darug is debated. Eora S61 has been used as the name for the coastal variety of Dharug / Darug, also known as the 'Sydney language' (Kohen 1993:15, 22; Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:140; Troy 2019:1). However, Eora S61 has also been described as a language separate from Dharug / Darug (Ross 1988).
abs_name: Other Australian Indigenous Languages, nec (Dharuk etc.)
location_info:
Dharug / Darug is located in the Sydney region, NSW. The inland variety extends west of the Georges River, from the Hawkesbury River in the north to Appin in the south (Attenbrow 2010:35). This includes Parramatta, Lane Cove River and Berowra Creek, and extends as far west as the Blue Mountains (Steel & Kohen 1996:223). The coastal variety extends from Port Jackson in the north, possibly as far as Broken Bay, to Botany Bay in the south and west to Parramatta (Attenbrow 2010:2010). This area is also described as Eora S61 Country.

Neighbouring languages include Darkinyung S65 and Kuringgai S62 to the north, Eora S61 to the east, Dharawal S59 and Gundungurra / Gandangara S60 to the south and Wiradjuri D10 to the west.

overview:
Wangkatja, Pindiini A102 and Wangkatha A12 are all listed as separate dialects of the Western Desert language A80 in this database but they appear to be very close to each other and hardly distinguishable. The WA Handbook, Glass (1990 p.c.) notes that the term Wangkatja is confusing, 'because all the Western Desert speaking Aborigines of the Eastern Goldfields and surrounding desert areas call themselves Wangkatja'.

Douglas (1990 p.c.) and Glass (1990 p.c.) point out that Wanggatha A12 from around Mt Margaret and Leonora is different to Wangkatja at Cundelee and Coonana.

Fasolo (2008) says that the Wangkatja people were known as the Nyanganyatjarra A17 people (also Puntutjarra people) because they used the word nyanganya ('this here'). However, Tindale lists Nagatadjara A17 as a separate group and locates it north-east of Wangkatja. In fact, it appears that Nyanganyatjarra is a sub-group of Wangkatja - Oates (1975:111), citing Glass and Hackett, says that Njanganjadjara A17 was originally at Mt Margaret, Wangkatja country, but its present location is north-east of Laverton.

Tindale's Pindiini may be the equivalent of Wangkatja or Wangkatha A12 - he lists Wanggada as an alternative name of Pindiini but it is treated as a separate dialect in this database on the basis of Tindale's distinct location for each of these. Between Pindiini A102 and Wangkatha, Tindale's map shows two other groups, Murunitja A8 and Tjeraridjal A7, but the validity of these groups is uncertain. Wangatha A12 or Wangkatja A103 may have been spoken there.

Fasolo (2008:1) notes that Cundeelee Wangka dialects have been referred to as Wangkatja. Hanson reports that speakers say Wangkatja is the same as Kuwarra A16 and that Kuwarra is also another name for Tjupan A31 (Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre 2008). According to Marmion (in Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre 2008), Wangkatja now refers to a speech variety spoken by Western Desert people around Laverton-Kalgoorlie.

The ABS treats Wangkatja as an alternative name of Wangkatha so Census data on Wangkatha may be relevant. Documentation on Wangkatha may also be relevant since the Thesaurus does not distinguish Wangkatja from Wangkatha. This database treats Wangkatja as a distinct variety, which is sometimes referred to as Cundeelee Wangka.
location_info: Cundelee and Coonana (WA Handbook) Eastern Goldfields, around the Linden/Mulgabbie area, Cundelee (Fasolo 2008) Contemporary location The people spread to the towns of Laverton, Leonora, Menzies, and then on down to other Goldfields towns where many of them still live today. (Fasolo 2008:1)

overview: According to Oates (1975:375), Douglas' meaning of the word ngurlu (i.e. 'fear', 'afraid') suggests this is not a dialect name, though she also notes Capell's (1963) reference to Tindale's comment that 'after 1890 Ngurlu was overwhelmed by the westward movement of Waljen A11 and Nangadadjara A17 tribes'. Based on the information available, Ngurlu is unlikely to be a language name.
location_info: Menzies to Malcolm; northwest to Mount Ida; east to Lake Raeside and Yerilla; at Lake Ballard. Their southern boundary lies at the change from their predominantly mulga country to the mallee Eucalypt country of the Maduwongga (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Alyawarr is an Arandic language C48 variety. Green et al. mention significant dialect variation in Alyawarr, especially between Lake Nash (Ilperrelhelam) and the western communities such as Antarrengeny and Wetenngerr in both vocabulary and grammatical constructions. These dialects are a result of Alyawarr people moving north to Ilperrelhelam in the twenties and thirties from the Sandover, as far south as Arltunga, to escape conflict and to be closer to work and rations (2019: 1).

The Alyawarr dictionary indicates dialectal differences where they occur (Green et al. 2019). Breen describes southern and northern Alyawarr phonology in separate sections (2001:56-59); he also notes that eastern form of Anmatyerr is closer to southern Alyawarr than with western Anmatyerr (2001:46-47)

Wilkins (in Henderson 2013:12) provides an overview of the Arandic languages with two major sub-groups: Artwe (~Urtwe) composed of Upper Arrernte (Eastern Arrernte, Western Arrernte C47, Alyawarr (C14), Anmatyerr C8.1">C8.1 ) and Lower Arrernte C29 (Lower South Arandic). The other major subgroup is called Artweye, with one member Kaytetye C13. See also Arrernte C8, Pertame C46; Lower Arrernte C29; Ayerrerenge G12; Antekerrepenhe C12 and Akarre C28.
location_info: an area roughly bounded by Hatches Creek, Utopia, MacDonald Downs and Ooratippra (Yallop 1977:3) Sandover, Bundey, Ooratippra, and Fraser creeks; Mount Swan, northern face of Hart Range, Plenty River north and west of Ilbala, Jervois Range, Mount Playford, Elkedra River; at MacDonald Downs and Huckitta (Tindale 1974). The general territorial association was to the south-eastern drainages of the Davenport Ranges and thence eastwards to Argadargada waterhole. Eastward limit of associations in the Argadargada waterhole area where associations changed to Ayerrereng. Northern limit of associations along the drainage divide in the Davenport ranges from Skinner Creek to Yaddanilla Creek. Canteen Creek was associated with Wakaya. Western limit of associations was Skinner Creek drainage. Murray Downs was associated with Alyawarr. Ali Curung was associated with Kaytetye (Harvey ASEDA 802).

overview: Wurumungu is a Pama Nyungan language from the Northern Territory. The classification of Warumungu is uncertain, however it is classified as 'Warumungu group' in various linguistic surveys. Warumungu shares vocabulary with neighbouring languages including Western Desert languages A80, also Warlpiri C15, Warlmanpa C17 and Kayteye C13 an Arandic language (Wafer, 1982).
location_info: Warumungu speakers live at Tennant Creek, to the north and east at Elliott, Kurntulpara, Ngurrara, Wogayala and Alroy Downs and on several oustations such as Likkapartta and Pingala; and to the south at Alekarenge and Karlinjarangi (Simpson 2002:3). Eastward limit: Bonney Creek and Kurrundi Creek drainages were associated with Warumungu. Whistleduck Creek drainage was associated with Wakaya. Rockhampton Downs homestead was associated with Warumungu. No14 bore was the western limit of Wakaya affiliations. Northward limit: There is no precise information on the northward limit. It was extrapolated on the basis of the information on the eastward and westward limits. Westward limit: The Ashburton Range south from Mt Grayling, The Whittington Range, The Short Range. Kartijirarrakanya Claypan appears to have been associated with Warlmanpa. Warrego Mine and Kunayungku OS were associated with Warumungu. The western associations extended south to approximately the level of the Davenport Ranges. Southward limit: Bonney Creek drainage was associated with Warumungu. Drainages heading southwards from the Younghusband and Davenport Ranges were associated with Kaytetye (Harvey ASEDA 802). Mount Grayling (Renner Springs) in the north; south to headwaters of Gosse River; east to Alroy and Rockhampton Downs, western boundary on edge of sand plain about 50 miles (80 km.), west of Tennant Creek (Tindale 1974).

overview: This is a dialect of Gunbarlang N69 according to Coleman (1982). Documentation on Gunbarlang N69 may be relevant.

See and use Nyangumarta A61.

'Most Nyangumarta speakers and others who study this language recognise two main dialects: inland or southern Nyangumarta (sometimes called Ngurlipartu) and coastal or northern Nyangumartu (sometimes called Walyirli). Though certain words are different between these two dialects, it's important to remember that they are very much alike and that Nyangumarta speakers still think of them as being part of the same language' (Geytenbeek et. al. 2015: viii).

Sharp's (2004:4) informants identify Pijikala, to the north near Lake Waukarlykarly, as one of four Nyangumarta A61 dialects. The others are reported to be Kuntal A98, Ngurlipartu A72 to the south, and Walyirli A73, the dialect spoken at Yandeyarra and the Twelve Mile Reserve on the outskirts of Port Hedland. From a linguistic perspective Sharp recognises two distinct types of Nyangumarta, Ngurlipartu A72 and Walyirli A73, which she refers to as northern coastal Nyangumarta and southern inland Nyangumarta respectively.
location_info: ... to the north near Lake Waukarlykarly (Sharp 2004:4).

overview:
According to the Kimberley Handbook, Nawurtu is the inland dialect of three Karajarri A64 dialects, the other two being Najanaja A106 on the coast and Nangu A105 in the middle. McGregor (2004:9) says that owners of the Nangu, Nawurtu and Najanaja language varieties regard them as types of Karajarri and use both the general and more specific terms in reference to their language.

McKelson (MS 2688) says that Capell, Worms and Nekes have made studies of Najanaja with reference made to inland Karajarri.
location_info: ... east of Bidyadanga (McKelson & Dodd 2007:191).

overview:
Von Brandenstein (1969, in Thieberger 1993), says Pidungu A40 has at least three dialects. Seen from Peak Hill, they are Ngarrka (east), Kurdun A119 (west) and Yirrakalan A120 (south but north of Meekatharra). There appears to be no language data supplied for these dialects.

Oates and Oates (1970) also make reference to Ngarrga(warngga) (A118) as a dialect of Bedengo A40 (though the other two names are not mentioned) and say that von Brandenstein collected vocabulary. Documentation for Birdungu A40 may be relevant.
location_info: ... east of Peak Hill (von Brandenstein, in Thieberger 1993).

overview:
According to the Kimberley Handbook, Nangu is the middle dialect of three Karajarri A64 dialects, the other two being Najanaja A106 on the coast and Nawurtu A107 from inland. McGregor (2004:9) says that owners of the Nangu, Nawurtu and Najanaja language varieties regard them as types of Karajarri and use both the general and more specific terms in reference to their language.

McKelson (1989) is principally concerned with the Nangu dialect of Karajarri.
location_info: ... located south east of Bidyadanga (McKelson & Dodd 2007:190).

overview: Pinkangarna does not seem to be a language or dialect name. Nash (in Sutton 1995:105) considers that Binkangarna (C21) applies to Mudburra C25 people from the semi-desert, and distinguishing them from their south-eastern neighbours. According to McConvell (2006 p.c.), the term Pinkangarna is no longer used, and it is either an alternative name for Mudburra C25 or is a dialect. It means 'river people' but it is not very clear which river it refers to.
location_info: West of Lake Woods; east of upper Victoria River; principally in the parallel sand dune desert southwest to near a native place called Morerinju on Winnecke Creek (Tindale 1974:222).

overview:
Previously Bunara A69 was treated as an alternative name for Ngardi. Tindale (1974) lists Bunara as an alternative name for Ngardi (as well as for Kokatja A68). However, both Oates and Oates (1970) and Oates (1975) treat Bunara and Ngardi as separate language varieties, and Capell (1940:425, 429) supplies distinct sets of language data for Ngardi (A121) and Buna:ra A69. Given this, Ngardi and Bunara A69 are now treated as distinct languages and a new record has been created for Bunara in AUSTLANG. The code A69 was originally assigned to Bunara; this is reinstated and the new code (A121) is assigned to Ngardi.

Some sources link Ngardi to Warlpiri C15, either as an alternative name (Oates and Oates 1970) or a dialect (Capell 1963). However, Capell (1940:429) gives language data for 'Ngadi' (contrasting with 'Ngardi' in Capell 1963) and the location he describes does not overlap with his 1963 location for Waljbiri C15. Laughren (2013 p.c.) makes a distinction between Ngardi and Ngardilypa C38, the latter being a dialect of Warlpiri, which she locates around 'the Granites about Tanami' (1996:2). This location appears to be between that of Ngardi (A121) and Warlpiri C15. Other sources link Ngardi to Kukatja A68. Watson, in Kleinert and Neale (2000:46), says that Ngardi and Kukatja are now referred to as Kutjungka ('at one') to express their common cultural heritage. Honeyman (2005:22) notes that many Ngardi speakers come from the Balgo area in which Kukatja is one of the primary languages.
location_info:
West of Walmanba, about WA border. East of Lake Gregory. (Oates 1975:133) ... about Lewis's Creek, immediately south of Sturt's Creek (Capell 1940:425).

The Ngardi speakers lived in an area roughly bounded by Balgo and the southern shore of Lake Gregory in the north, the NT-WA border in the east, the Mangkayi area (north of Lake Mackay) in the south and just east of the Canning Stock Route in the west (Cataldi ASEDA 0737).

Sandhill country west of the Tanami track, from Chilla Well, the Granites, and Gardiner Range extending west into Western Australia at Ima Ima (n.n. Ngaima ngaima) on Sturt Creek, to Balgo Hill (and the Pallotine Mission), also to Manggai, an unidentified water; they go south to near Milidjipi (129°40' E x 22°3'S) and to Tekkari, north of Lake Mackay (129°1'E x 21°50'S). These are two known native waters in otherwise unnamed country; at Lakes Hazlett, Lucas, White, and Wills. Some important but as yet unlocalized waters include Pinbin (near Lake Lucas), Lerauli, Ngandalara and Pinkatjana (near Emily Springs), Pindiri, Tjaldjiwan, Inindi (near Lake White), and Rabi (between Lakes Lucas and White). Their southern territory extends into large areas covered by mulga scrub (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Kalaw Kawaw Ya is the language of the Gudaw Maluligal Nation of the Top Western Islands of Zenadth Kes (Torres Strait). It is also located on northern tip of Cape York, QLD. It is a variety of Kala Lagaw Ya Y1. The name Kalaw Kawaw Ya means 'western Island language' (Ford & Ober 1991:118).  

Zenadth Kes is a name commonly used instead of the non-Indigenous name 'Torres Strait'. It was created by Elder and linguist Adhi Ephraim Bani, who wanted to redefine the non-Indigenous name by combining traditional names for the four winds that pass through the region (Torres Strait Island Regional Council 2026).

Kalaw Kawaw Ya is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Some available resources include Kevin Ford and Dana Ober's (1991) A sketch of Kalaw Kawaw Ya and Sidney Ray's (2003) Dictionary of Torres Strait languages. The first language program was run in the 1970s. Since 2008, Tagai State College has supported the teaching of Zenadth Kes traditional languages, and has worked with the Torres Strait Traditional Languages Centre to support language revitalisation (Torres Strait Traditional Language Centre 2026).

In 2015 the Torres Strait Regional Authority, Tagai State College and communities across Zenadth Kes formed a 'language reference group' in order to coordinate language revitalisation and develop a Traditional Language Plan (Zenadth Kes Language Symposium 2024). Since then, Community Language Teams, languages programs and cultural activities have occurred in both Meriam Mir Y3 and Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 varieties (Torres Strait Traditional Languages Plan 2016-2019). In 2023 the Torres Strait Traditional Languages Association was established to continue to support and revitalise Zenadth Kes traditional languages.

Torres Strait Creole P2 is a language shared across all of Zenadth Kes (Torres Strait Traditional Languages Plan 2016-2019). The western variety of Torres Strait Creole P2 shares features with Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 (Tudor-Smith 2024:148). Torres Strait Creole P2 is used to identify Torres Strait Islanders in Collections Online. This does not imply that all Torres Strait Islanders are speakers of Torres Strait Creole P2. Sources relating to Torres Strait Creole P2 may be relevant.

 Kalaw Kawaw Ya is a Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 (Western Torres) language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 is the traditional name for the Western Torres language subgroup, which includes the following Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 varieties: Kalaw Kawaw Ya, Mabuyag Y239, Kulkalgaw Ya Y4 and Kawalgaw Ya Y5. Waru lag Y227 may be another Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 variety (Laade 1968:145).

The classification of Kala Lagaw Ya Y1 as a Pama-Nyungan language has been debated. It shares linguistic features, such as vocabulary and grammar, with Papuan languages as well as Pama-Nyungan languages. Contemporarily, it is largely believed to be a Pama-Nyungan language (see Alpher et. al. 2008).

Note: the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) does not make a distinction between Kalaw Lagaw Ya Y1 and Kalaw Kawaw Ya Y2. Census data may cover both varieties.
thes_peop_head: Western Torres Strait Islander people Y2
location_info:
Kalaw Kawaw Ya is located on the islands of Saibai, Boigu and Dauan in Zenadth Kes (Torres Strait) and on the mainland in Seisia and Bamaga, QLD (Round & Stirling 2015:253; Torres Strait Traditional Language Centre 2026).

Neighbouring languages include Torres Strait Creole P2, Waru lag Y227 to the northeast, Meriam Mir Y3 to the east, Mabuyag Y239 and Kawalgaw Ya Y5 to the south, and Kulkalgaw Ya Y4 to the southeast.

overview:
Marlpa (and variants) has been used in different ways by different sources - as an alternative name for Kalarku A2 (O'Grady, MS 3799) and Ngadjumaya A3 (Douglas 1968 and Oates 1975), and to refer to a language variety distinct from both of these.

Tindale (1974:243) reports that malba (A110) means 'circumcised and subincised ones' and is a 'name applied by Wudjari W41 to Kalaako A2 and other immediately northern tribes' (i.e. Kalamaia A4 and Ngadjunmaia A3). However, von Brandenstein (1970:3-4) says it means 'man' and identifies it as the name of one of six language varieties in the Dundas District area (the others being Mirning (Eucla) A9, Fraser Range A74, Norseman A99, Windaga A111 and Kallaagu A2).

Von Brandenstein (1980:2) comments that 'it will be difficult to extract the different components of the (Dundas District) languages...from the mixed language now called Ngadju A3 which is still spoken...' Von Brandenstein (1970:3-4) mentions there being 14 remaining speakers of Marlba (A110), which suggests that language data has been recorded.

A wordlist taken by Daisy Bates, titled 'Native vocabularies - Balladonia area', may contain Marlpa language data as it matches, in part, the location reported by von Brandenstein. Confusingly, though, von Brandenstein (1970:4, PMS 2143) also says that 'the location given by Capell (1963) A.25 is correct', but this is Capell's 'Ngadjunma'.

Oates (1975) explains that 'von Brandenstein calls this dialect Marlba after the word for 'man', and the modern polyglot of all the dialects he calls Ngadju and Ngadju(n)maja'. As most sources treat Ngadjunma, Ngadju and Ngadjumaya as variants of the same language variety A3, distinguishing between the original Marlba variety and the modern day Ngadjumaya is likely to be very difficult. Consequently, while catalogue records containing the Marlpa heading will ideally refer to the distinct language variety which preceded modern Ngadjumaya, they may in fact relate to modern-day Ngadjumaya A3, or even Kalarku A2.
location_info: Rock-holes and soaks around Balladonia, reaching north to Kopai Cliffs with the Murrunidja as neighbours and south to Israelite Bay. The location given by Capell (1963) A.25 is correct. 14 speakers of varying quality left. (von Brandenstein 1970:3-4).

overview: This name appears in Berndt (1959) as well as Capell (1963) and Oates and Oates (1970) but there appears to be no linguistic information available on this language.

Natingero is listed as an alternative name of Kalaamaya A4 by Tindale (1974) and O'Grady et al. (1966). However, Dixon (2007 p.c.) treats them as distinct languages on account of their sharing only 43 per cent vocabulary. Similarly, David Nash's comparison of Adam's word list 'Natingero tribe' in Curr with a Kalaamaya word list of gathered by Tindale shows only 36 per cent common vocabulary.
location_info: Two hundred miles north-east of Newcastle (Adam 1886).

overview:
Wadi Wadi D4 is the language of the Wadi Wadi D4 People of Swan Hill, VIC. It has one variety that shares the same name: Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67. These languages are often written as Wadi Wadi (Swan Hill) D4 and Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 to distinguish them from each other.

The name Wadi Wadi follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, wadi means 'no' (Tindale 1974:156). This distinguishes Wadi Wadi D4 and Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 from similar neighbouring languages.

Wadi Wadi D4 is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language projects have been undertaken in collaboration with organisations including Tati Tati Kaiejin (2022), Victorian Aboriginal Corporation for Languages (VACL 2026) and WCC Language Program (2021). Language resources have been developed, including Brendan Kennedy's (2014) Wangilatha Wangu nga Kiyawatha (Singing Songs and Telling Stories) released in Dadi Dadi S28, Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8, Latji Latji S23 and Wadi Wadi D4.

Wadi Wadi D4 shares strong social relationships with Latji Latji S23, Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8, Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67, Yitha Yitha D7, Dadi Dadi S28 and Paakantyi / Paakantji / Barkindji D12 (Blake et. al. 2011:25).

Wadi Wadi D4 is a Kulin language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It has one variety: Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67. There may be another variety called PuRa-PuRa (see Burabura D68), however this is unconfirmed (Blake et. al. 2011:1, 4). Wadi Wadi D4 is a member of the Western Victorian (Western Kulin) language group (Blake & Reid 1998:4). Within the Western Victorian group, it is a member of the Mathi (see Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8) subgroup along with Latji Latji S23 and Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 (Blake et. al. 2011:1). This may also include Weki Weki S33 and Nyeri Nyeri (Jari Jari S24)(Blake et. al. 2011:1). Other Western Victorian languages include the Wergaia S17 subgroup and the Wemba (see Wemba Wemba D1) subgroup (Hercus 1992: 1; Blake & Reid 1998:4).

Sources relating to Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 may be relevant.

Wadi Wadi D4 should not be confused with Wodi Wodi (Southern Dharawal S58), a language of the Illawarra region, NSW.
location_info:
Wadi Wadi D4 is located around Swan Hill, VIC. It extends north from Swan Hill to Tyntynder, west to Woorinen and Lake Tyrrell, northeast to Piangil and east to Stoney Crossing and Moolpa, NSW (Tindale 1974:208; Blake et. al. 2011:3-4; Tati Tati Kaiejin 2022).

The Wadi Wadi D4 language of Swan Hill is more closely associated with the Victorian side of the Murray River, while Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is closely associated with the New South Wales side of the Murray River (Blake et. al. 2011:4).

Neighbouring languages include Dadi Dadi S28 to the northwest, Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8 and Nari Nari D9 to the northeast, Wemba Wemba D1 to the south and Wergaia S17 to the west.

overview:
Ngunuru ('middle') Wajarri is the variety from around Meekatharra, south of Nharnu and probably extending further east, maybe part way to Wiluna and Western Desert country. This could also be called 'Mileura Wajarri' A114, i.e. using a station as a reference point. Marmion (2015 p.c.) says this is likely.

The Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation web site lists Ngunuru (A112) among 'some of' the Wajarri A39 dialects, the others being Birdungu A40, Nharnu A115, Nhugarn A71, Byro A113 and Mileura A114. Marmion (1996:7), however, only describes three dialects: 'Southern Wajarri' A39 (a term coined by Marmion to disambiguate this unnamed variety from the other two dialects), Nhugarn A71 and Birdungu A40 / Ngunuru (A112). Note that Marmion conflates Birdungu and Ngunuru, treated as distinct dialects by Bundiyarra. Marmion explains that this dialect of Wajarri A39 is known to the Nhugarn A71 as Birdungu A40 but that speakers refer to themselves as Ngunuru (A112), a term meaning 'middle', referencing their position between the Western Desert people and the other varieties of Wajarri.
location_info: Ngunuru Wajarri around Belele station (Elefsiniotis of Irra Wangga - Geraldton Language Programme, 2007 p.c.)

overview:
Breen (1988:1) says there are three dialects of the same language as Bularnu G12.1">G12.1: Dhidhanu G42, Baringkirri and Indjiladji G52, cautioning that the variant form of the last, Indjilandji, is also the name of a neighbouring language to the north G14.

Brammal (1991:2) notes the existence of these near-identically named languages, but says he is doubtful that Injilaji G52 is actually distinct from Bularnu.
location_info: Headingly (Breen 1988:[1])

overview: The Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation web site lists Byro (A113) among 'some of' the Wajarri / Wadjarri A39 dialects, the others being Birdungu A40, Nharnu A115, Nhugarn A71, Mileura A114 and Ngunuru A112. Marmion (1996:6-7) does not include Byro Wajarri in his description of Wajarri A39 dialects. Marmion (2015 p.c.) notes that in more recent times Wajarri varieties have been referred to by station names in the area, such as Byro station and Mileura station, leading to some names existing in parallel with older names. He says that Byro Wajarri is probably equivalent to Nhugarn A71.
location_info: Byro station (Elefsiniotis 2007 p.c.)

overview:
Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is the language of the Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 People of Piangil, VIC. It is a variety of Wadi Wadi D4 and shares its name. These languages are often written as Wadi Wadi (Swan Hill) D4 and Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 to distinguish them from each other.

The name Wadi Wadi follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, wadi means 'no' (Tindale 1974:156). This distinguishes Wadi Wadi D4 and Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 from similar neighbouring languages.

Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is also referred to as Piangil, the name of the town where Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is located (Tindale 1974:208; Clark 2005). It is included in the heading name to distinguish this variety from Wadi Wadi D4. Piangil may be derived from the traditional word bandjel meaning 'Murray Cod' (Clark & Heydon 2002:176), however this is unconfirmed.

Wadi Wadi D4, which is related to Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language projects have been undertaken in collaboration with organisations including Tati Tati Kaiejin (2022), Victorian Aboriginal Corporation for Languages (VACL 2026) and WCC Language Program (2021). Language resources have been developed, including Brendan Kennedy's (2014) Wangilatha Wangu nga Kiyawatha (Singing Songs and Telling Stories) released in Dadi Dadi S28, Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8, Latji Latji S23 and Wadi Wadi D4.

Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 shares strong social relationships with Latji Latji S23, Wadi Wadi D4, Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D67, Yitha Yitha D7, Dadi Dadi S28 and Paakantyi / Paakantji / Barkindji D12 (Blake et. al. 2011:25).

Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is a Kulin language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a variety of Wadi Wadi D4. Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is a member of the Western Victorian (Western Kulin) language group (Blake & Reid 1998:4). Within the Western Victorian group, it is a member of the Mathi (see Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8) subgroup along with Latji Latji S23 and Wadi Wadi D4 (Blake et. al. 2011:1). This may also include Weki Weki S33 and Nyeri Nyeri (Jari Jari S24)(Blake et. al. 2011:1). Other Western Victorian languages include the Wergaia S17 subgroup and the Wemba (see Wemba Wemba D1) subgroup (Hercus 1992: 1; Blake & Reid 1998:4).

Previously, Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 has been described as the same language as Weki Weki S33 based on their shared location around Piangil (Oates & Oates 1970:142; Blake et. al. 2011:3, 215). However, there is not enough evidence to confirm that they are the same language (Blake et. al. 2011:3).

Sources relating to Wadi Wadi D4 may be relevant.

Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 should not be confused with Wodi Wodi (Southern Dharawal S58), a language of the Illawarra region, NSW.
location_info:
Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is located around Piangil, VIC. It extends over the Murray River into New South Wales, around the Lower Lachlan and Murrumbidgee Rivers (Blake et. al. 2011:4).

The Wadi Wadi D4 language of Swan Hill is more closely associated with the Victorian side of the Murray River, while Wadi Wadi (Piangil) D67 is closely associated with the New South Wales side of the Murray River (Blake et. al. 2011:4).

Neighbouring languages include Dadi Dadi S28 to the northwest, Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8 and Nari Nari D9 to the northeast, Wemba Wemba D1 to the south and Wergaia S17 to the west.

overview: Oates (1975:376) says that Tindale's mapping is the only available information, but there is a word list by Tindale.
location_info: East of Lake Raeside from Malcolm, Morgans, Laverton, and Burtville, southeast to Edjudina Soaks, n.n. ['I:tjuruna], ['tjortjor] or ['manda 'tjukur] (mopoke totem) and Lake Lightfoot; at Lake Carey; east to beyond Lake Minigwal and a native place, not fixed, called ['Winbalj]. In the 1890s they shifted south to Kalgoorlie in a general southwestward movement (Tindale 1974).

overview:
This name is mentioned in Berndt (1942:328) who mentions the connection between 'the spinifex people at Laverton' and the 'tribes to their west, such as the 'Waul'wu'lu', 'Wɔrda and 'Maŋ'u' (A34). Capell's Linguistic Survey (1963) lists the last of these, Mangu/'Maŋ'u.

It seems that the only data available on Mangu comprises three pronouns listed by Brown (MS 1349), who does not quote the source and says 'precise location unknown, but probably somewhere in central WA'. On Berndt's map (1942), 'Maŋ'u (A34) is west of Lake Nabberu and Lake Gregory, not west of Laverton as stated in his text (1942:328).

Mangu might be a mishearing of Marrngu, a group name covering languages found north of Lake Gregory, such as Nyangumarta A61, and Brown's data may be from one or a combination of Marrngu languages. Thieberger lists Mangu as a name associated with Western Desert A80 language (1993: 397).
location_info: Northeast of Peak Hill (map in Oates & Oates 1970). ... west of Laverton (Berndt 1942:328).

overview:
Wemba Wemba is the language of the Wamba Wemba People of the Murray-Mallee region, NSW / VIC. It has one variety: Barababaraba D5. Wemba Wemba is also used as the name of a language subgroup. The name Wemba Wemba follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, wemba means 'no' (Clark 2005). This distinguishes Wemba Wemba from similar neighbouring languages.

Wemba Wemba is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language projects have been undertaken in collaboration with organisations including Wiradjuri Condobolin Corporation Language Program (WCCLP 2021), Yarkuwa Indigenous Knowledge Centre (2026) and Wamba Wemba Aboriginal Corporation (2026). Language resources have been developed, including a dictionary app and website (Yarkuwa Indigenous Knowledge Centre 2026). Wemba Wemba has been taught in schools in Swan Hill, Deniliquin and surrounding areas.

Wemba Wemba is a Kulin language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Western Victorian (Western Kulin) language group (Hercus 1992:1). Wemba Wemba has one variety: Barababaraba D5. Nari Nari D9 may also be a variety of Wemba Wemba (Hercus 1992:3), however this is unconfirmed. Within the Western Victorian group, these three languages make up the Wemba subgroup, named after Wemba Wemba. Other Western Victorian languages include the Wergaia S17 subgroup and the Mathi (see Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8) subgroup (Hercus 1992: 1; Blake & Reid 1998:4).
abs_name: Other Australian Indigenous Languages, nec (Wamba Wamba)
location_info:
Wemba Wemba is located in the Murray-Mallee region, in both New South Wales and Victoria. It extends from Booroorban and Moulamein in the north, south across the Murray River to Boort and Charlton in Victoria, east to Deniliquin and west to Swan Hill. This area includes Kerang, Lake Boga, the Loddon River and the Avoca River (Capell 1963:15).

Neighbouring languages include Nari Nari D9 to the north, Barababaraba D5 to the east, Wergaia S17 to the south and Wadi Wadi D4 to the west.

overview:
See and use Malgana A65.

McKelson (nd) describes two dialects of Malgana A65: 'riverside Malgana' in the north-east, adjacent to the Fitzroy River, and 'bush Mangala', south-east of La Grange Mission. He does not provide data or descriptions of these dialects, though he makes notes in 1989 (Series 5, Item 2) that may correspond to dialectal differences.

Weber (2009:3) reports that Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre refers to these dialects according to the word for closing a discussion or event: 'Kakutu/Kakurtu' (riverside) A122 and 'Ngulatu/Ngulartu' (bush) A123. Weber notes that, while the differences between these dialects have not been documented, the Mangarla dialect described in Hudson (1973) differs phonologically from that described in McKelson (1989, Series 5, Item 4).
location_info: ... spoken to the north east, in an area adjacent to the Fitzroy river (McKelson, nd).

overview: Ngarinyman speakers describe varieties of Ngarinyman including Wurlayi (Wurli) (http://dobes.mpi.nl/projects/jaminjung/languages/, viewed on 19/05/17). This is a dialect of Ngarinyman C27 according to McConvell (1980). Documentation on Ngarinyman may be relevant.
Western Mudburra is one of the Mudburra C25 dialects. Documentation on Mudburra C25 may be relevant.

The Tasmanian languages/dialects records are sparse. Crowley and Dixon (1981:402) say that Little Swanport could be a dialect of the Oyster Bay T2 / Big River T8 language. Crowley (1993:54) concludes from examination of vocabulary lists and comments from colonial observations about who could and who could not understand each other, that at least eight separate languages and possibly as many as twelve belong to Tasmania. Crowley and Dixon (1981:404) conclude there is no evidence to indicate a single Tasmanian language family, available evidence indicates two, four or even eight distinct families. Bowern (2012) groups twelve languages into four language macro-families (northeastern, Oyster Bay, southeastern (Bruny) and western) using methods from evolutionary biology to systematically investigate vocabularies, from thirty five language lists. Crowley and Dixon (1981:402-403) compare collected vocabularies from fifteen regions. This database assigns reference names for Tasmania based on this regional list. See also Northern T1; Oyster Bay T2; North-western T3; Northern Midlands T4; South-eastern T5; Macquarie Harbour T6; Ben Lomond T7; Big River T8; Cape Portland T9; South-western T10; Robbin Island T11; Circular Head T12; Port Sorrell T13 and Piper River T14. The areas defined as Little Swanport and Oyster Bay T2 in Crowley and Dixon's map (1981:394) roughly coincides with the area defined as Paredarerne by Horton in the AIATSIS map of Aboriginal Australia. Little Swanport language data, along with historical sources from all Tasmanian language varieties form the basis of palawa kani language T16.
location_info: TAS

overview:
Barababaraba is the language of the Barapa Barapa People of the Murray-Mallee region, NSW / VIC. It is a variety of Wemba Wemba D1. The name Barababaraba follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, baraba means 'no' (Clark 2005). This distinguishes Barababaraba from similar neighbouring languages.

Wemba Wemba D1, which is related to Barababaraba, is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Numerous language projects have been undertaken in collaboration with organisations including Wiradjuri Condobolin Corporation Language Program (WCCLP 2021), Yarkuwa Indigenous Knowledge Centre (2026) and Wamba Wemba Aboriginal Corporation (2026). Language resources have been developed, including a dictionary app and website (Yarkuwa Indigenous Knowledge Centre 2026). Wemba Wemba D1 has been taught in schools in Swan Hill, Deniliquin and surrounding areas.

Barababaraba is a Kulin language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Wurm 1972:135). It is a member of the Western Victorian (Western Kulin) language group (Hercus 1992:1). Barababaraba is a variety of Wemba Wemba D1. Nari Nari D9 may also be a Wemba Wemba D1 variety (Hercus 1992:3), however this is unconfirmed. Within the Western Victorian group, these three languages make up the Wemba subgroup, named after Wemba Wemba D1. Other Western Victorian languages include the Wergaia S17 subgroup and the Mathi (see Mutti Mutti / Muthi Muthi D8) subgroup (Hercus 1992: 1; Blake & Reid 1998:4).

Previously, Barababaraba has been classified as a Yotayotic (see Yorta Yorta D2) language (O'Grady et. al. 1966:48). However, its classification as a Kulin language is more widely accepted.

The relationship between Barababaraba and Burabura D68 is uncertain. Burabura D68 is recorded as an alternative name for Barababaraba (see O'Grady et. al. 1966:47-8; Oates & Oates 1970:138; Tindale 1974:191-2). However, it is also described as a separate language from Barababaraba (see Beveridge 1883; Capell 1963:3; Mathews MS 1981).

Sources relating to Burabura D68 may be relevant.
location_info:
Barababaraba is located in the Murray-Mallee region, NSW / VIC. Parts of this area are described as Wemba Wemba D1 Country. It extends from Carrathool and Hay in the north, as far south as parts of Loddon and Campaspe, east to Brassi and Conargo, and west to Kerang and Lake Boga (Capell 1963:3; Barapa 2026). This area includes the southern tributaries of the Murrumbidgee River, Gannawarra and Gunbower.

Neighbouring languages include Wiradjuri D10 to the north, Nari Nari D9 to the northwest, Yorta Yorta D2 to the east, Dja Dja Wurrung S31.1 to the south and Wemba Wemba D1 to the west.

overview: McConvell (1980) distinguishes three dialects of Ngarinman (C27): Eastern Ngarinman C32, Bilinara N36, and Wurlayi C37. Widijburru et al. (2010:13) mention the existence of two different forms for some items in their plant and animal dictionary. They point out that this could reflect two varieties 'more strongly differentiated in the past' (north-west vs. south-east), or they could be relics of the extinct Nyiwanawu C45 language. They also say the different forms could 'represent the western form of the Ngarinyman language referred to as Wurlayi Ngarinyman by some speakers and linguists' though it is not clear if this is the same or additional to the north-west/south-east distinction mentioned earlier.
location_info: The general affiliation was to the drainage of Wickham and Humbert Rivers above Yarralin (Harvey ASEDA 802). Upper Victoria River, about Jasper Creek; west of Victoria River Downs; south to Mount Sanford (n.n. Mun-jan), west to Limbunya, chiefly on Wickham River. (Tindale 1974). Ngarinyman country traditionally extends across much of what is now called Judbarra/Gregory National Park, it includes areas such as Bullita, Yarralin, Lingara, Limestone Gorge, Bulla, Amanbidji, parts of Victoria River Downs, Humbert River, east Baines River and the Wickham River. (Widijburru et al. 2010:11).

overview:
See and use Malgana A65.

McKelson (nd) describes two dialects of Malgana A65: 'riverside Malgana' in the north-east, adjacent to the Fitzroy River, and 'bush Mangala', south-east of La Grange Mission. He does not provide data or descriptions of these dialects, though he makes notes in 1989 (Series 5, Item 2) that may correspond to dialectal differences. Weber (2009:3) reports that Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre refers to these dialects according to the word for closing a discussion or event: 'Ngulatu/Ngulartu' (bush) and 'Kakutu/Kakurtu' (riverside) A122.

Weber notes that, while the differences between these dialects have not been documented, the Mangarla dialect described in Hudson (1973) differs phonologically from that described in McKelson (1989, Series 5, Item 4).
location_info: ... spoken southeast of [La Grange] mission (McKelson, MS 2687)

overview: This is a dialect of the Western Desert language A80. Note that in the Ngaanyatjarra A38 dialect of the Western Desert language, Kuwarra means 'hold on, wait'. It is also mentioned as a language name in Thieberger (1993:189), although no language data is provided.
location_info: South of Agnew (on Liberman's map 1978). From Morgans and Leonora west to Mount Ida, Lake Barlee, and Sandstone; north to Gidgee, Mount Sir Samuel, and Lake Darlot; east to Mount Zephyr; northwestern boundary west of Sandstone (Tindale 1974).

overview:
There appear to be several dialects of Wajarri / Wadjarri though the details are uncertain. According to Vaso Elefsiniotis of the Irra Wangga - Geraldton Language Program (2007 p.c.), the current understanding is that there are five recognised dialects of Wajarri (A39): Byro Wajarri in the east around Byro plains; Boolardy or central Wajarri around Boolardy/Wooleen stations; Ngunuru Wajarri around Belele station; Birdungu Wajarri to the north-east of Boolardy where the Murchison and Gascoyne Rivers begin; and Nharnu Wajarri. Elefsiniotis also comments that Birdungu is the name given by others to the Wajarri people who traditionally lived at the eastern or north-eastern boundary of Wajarri country, depending on the observer's perspective.

According to Marmion (1996:6-7) there are at least three dialects of Wajarri (A39). The dialect which covers most of Wajarri country appears to have no particular name other than Wajarri (Marmion uses 'Southern Wajarri' (and occasionally 'Central Wajarri') to disambiguate it from other varieties). The other two are Nhugarn A71 and Birdungu A40. Marmion (2007 p.c.) later says that Birdungu A40 is a compass term and is used to refer to people from around Meekatharra who are not Wajarri (or at least, not central Wajarri).

The Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation web site lists 'some' of the Wajarri (A39) dialects as Birdungu A40, Nharnu A115, Nhugarn A71, Byro A113, Mileura A114 and Ngunuru A112. Marmion (2015 p.c.) notes that in more recent times Wajarri (A39) varieties have been referred to by station names in the area, such as Byro station and Mileura station. In this way, some names may exist in parallel with older names: Byro Wajarri A113 is probably equivalent to Nhugarn A71, Mileura Wajarri A114 to Ngunuru A112. He also notes the ambiguous nature of the name Birdungu, meaning 'easterners'. Marmion says that more recently it has been used to refer to Ngunuru A112 but that it may also include Nharnu A115, this likely being the case for von Brandenstein's use of the term.

Watjanti (W13) may also be a dialect of Wajarri / Wadjarri. Douglas (1981:199) says that a comparison of Curr's Watchandie W13 data is obviously related to Watjarri (A39). Blevins (2001:3), though, says that Watchandi W13 is a dialect of Nhanda W14. Muliara  (W18) is another possible dialect of Wajarri / Wadjarri. Marmion (2006 p.c.) says that mulyara means 'east' and it could refer to a dialect of Wajarri A39 or a Western Desert language A80 variety, based on what Tindale (1974) and Douglas (1981) say.

Jaburu (W55) has also been linked to Wajarri / Wadjarri as a dialect, though its identity is uncertain as the name means 'north' in many languages of area. Dixon (2002) lists Ngarluwangka as a possible dialect of Watjarri (A39) but notes that it may be a separate language. This may in fact be Ngarla A48, previously known as Ngarlawangka. The locations appear to be adjacent.
location_info:
... the country originally inhabited by the Wajarri appears to have extended from between the Wooramel and Gascoyne Rivers south to between the Murchison River and the Geraldton-Mt. Magnet road; in the west it approached the coastal highway and in the east it extended to around Mileura Station (Marmion 1996:2).

North to the hills overlooking the head of the Lyons River, Teano Range, Mount Isabella, Waldburg Range; on upper Gascoyne River west of Three Rivers; at Erivilla and Milgun; south to Cheangwa and the Roderick and upper Sanford rivers (Tindale 1974).

... along the upper reaches of the Murchison river, from around Yallalong Station in the west, to near Meekatharra in the east, from north of Mt Augustus, to south of Talarang Peak (sic, gazetted as Tallering Peak) (Mackman 2011:231).

Contemporary location: Carnarvon, Geraldton, Mullewa, Northampton, Meekatharra, and Yulga Jinna Community and Pia Wadjarri on traditional Wajarri land (Mackman 2011:227).

overview:
Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula is the language of the Ngarimoro (Ngarrimowro) and Bangerang S40 people of the Murray River region, NSW/VIC. It is a language of the Yortayortic subgroup (see Yorta Yorta D2) and a Bangerang S40 traditional people group. Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula community recognise multiple spellings. The two main preferred spellings are represented in the language name heading.

The name Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, jabula or yabula means 'no' (Tindale 1974:207). This distinguishes Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula from similar neighbouring languages.

Ngarimoro (Ngarrimowro) is a Bangerang S40 traditional group alongside Moirathban, Toolinyagan, Wolithiga, Kailthban, Angootheraban and the Pikkolatpan (VACL 2026).

Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula is a language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Yortayortic (see Yorta Yorta D2) subgroup, which includes Yorta Yorta D2 and Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula (Bowern 2023), Bangerang S40 and possibly Kwat Kwat S97 (Bowe & Morey 1999:3; Bowe 2002:140). The Yortayortic subgroup shares only a small number of linguistic features with surrounding subgroups, so it is often referred to as a language isolate (Bowe & Morey 1999:4).

The relationship between Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula and Yorta Yorta D2 is uncertain. Contemporarily, Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula and Yorta Yorta D2 are described as closely related languages, both belonging to the same subgroup (Bowe & Morey 1999:3; Bowern 2023). Additionally, Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula has been described as a variety of Yorta Yorta D2 (Bowe 2002:122). Due to a low number of shared linguistic features (i.e. vocabulary), the classification of Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula as a variety of Yorta Yorta D2 is uncertain (Bowe & Morey 1999:5).
location_info:
Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula is located on the Murray River, NSW/VIC. It extends on both sides of the Murray River from Deniliquin, NSW, in the north to Yielima, VIC, in the south, Tocumwal in the east to Mathoura in the west (RH Mathews in Bowe & Morey 1999:132).

Neighbouring languages include Wiradjuri D10 to the northeast, Taungurung S37 to the south and Bangerang S40 and Yorta Yorta D2 to the west.

overview:
The status of this dialect is not clear. Some treat it as an alternative name of Ngaanyatjarra A38, while Fasolo (2008) says that the Wangkatja A103 people were known as the Nyanganyatjarra people because they used the word nyanganya ('this here').

Tindale lists Nagatadjara (A17) as a separate group and locates them north-east of Wangkatja A103.

Oates (1975:111), citing Glass and Hackett, says that Njanganjadjara (A17) was originally at Mt Margaret, Wangkatja country, but its present location is north-east of Laverton.

A number of items with 'in Ngaanyatjarra' A38 in their titles are described as being on Nangadadjara / Nyanganyatjara in MURA (hence the question marks for the documentation score). See also Western Desert language A80.
location_info: East of Lake Carey and Burtville to about Jubilee and Plumridge Lakes; northeast to Bailey, Virginia, and Newland Ranges. At Lakes Yeo and Rason and at Bartlett Soak. Moved westward, between 1890 and 1900, to Burtville and Laverton (Tindale 1974).

overview: Kiyajarra is located south of Lake Disappointment in Berndt (1959), Tonkinson (1991) and Walsh (1981), but according to Tindale, this is not the original location of Keiadjara (A52). Tindale reports that the location given by Berndt (1959) is a place on the Keiadjara (A52) group's post-1930 westward movement into settled country. See also Western Desert language A80.
location_info: Southeast of the Mandjildjara territory and south and east of the Potidjara, in territory not identified except as WESTERN AUSTRALIA extending east from Kolajuru which is unidentified except as being several days walk southeast of Tjundutjundu (Well 30) on Canning Stock Route. Their territory may extend as far east as longitude 127° or beyond since Ngadadjara have contact with people whom they call Mangawara (a general term for shifting people who carry treasures tied in their hair chignons (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Kukatja A68 and Kukatja (C7) are described as separate dialects of the Western Desert language A80. Hansen and Hansen write that the Kukatja (A68) people who settled at Balgo Hills were Pintupi C10, who travelled north in the early 20th century, to where the Catholic Mission was later established. They were called Kukatja by Walmatjari A66 and others with the translation 'those who use the word "kuka" (for meat)' (1975:22).

According to Marmion (2005 p.c.), Kukatja people (C7) call themselves Luritja C7.1">C7.1 these days. Another group known as Mayutjarra, Ngalia C2 and Kukatja C7 were located east of Pintupi country, to the west of Haasts Bluff (Hansen and Hansen, 1975:22).

Tindale wrote that Matuntara (i.e. Hansens' Mayutjarra) is sometimes considered as a southern group of the Kukatja (C7) (1974:231).

Note that items on Kukatja (C7) may be described as being about Kukatja A68 or Kokatha C3 in MURA. Documentation for Kukatja (C7) may also be found under Luritja C7.1">C7.1 and Pintupi C10.
location_info: West of Gosse Range and Palm Valley on the south MacDonnell Ranges; south to Tempe Downs; southwest to Lake Amadeus, George Gill Range, Cleland Hills (Mer-andji), Inindi near Mount Forbes, and Thomas Reservoir (Alala); on upper Palmer, Walker, and Rudall creeks (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Kwat Kwat is the name of the Kwat Kwat people of the Murray-Goulburn region, VIC. The language of the Kwat Kwat people is Yorta Yorta D2 (VACL 2026). Kwat Kwat may also be a language name. The name Kwat Kwat follows the reduplication pattern of many Australian language names, where one word is repeated. Here, kwat means 'no' (Clark 2011). This distinguishes Kwat Kwat from similar neighbouring peoples and languages.

Kwat Kwat is a Yorta Yorta D2 traditional group, along with Kaitheban, Wollithiga, Moira, Ulupna, Bangerang S40, Yalaba Yalaba and Ngurai-illamwurrung S83 (VACL 2026).

Kwat Kwat may also be a language name. However, its relationship to surrounding language subgroups is uncertain (Bowe 2002:140). Kwat Kwat may be a language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowe & Morey 1999:5). It is most likely a member of the Yortayortic (see Yorta Yorta D2) subgroup, which includes Yorta Yorta D2 and Jabulajabula / Yabula Yabula S38 (Bowern 2023) and Bangerang S40 (Bowe & Morey 1999:3; Bowe 2002:140). It could be a part of a neighbouring subgroup, however its membership in the Yortayortic subgroup is more widely accepted (Bowe 2002:140). The Yortayortic subgroup shares only a small number of linguistic features with surrounding subgroups, so it is often referred to as a language isolate (Bowe & Morey 1999:4).

The relationship between Kwat Kwat, Bangerang S40 and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 has been debated. Kwat Kwat was previously listed under Bangerang S40, formally 'Bangerang / Kwat Kwat / Waveroo'. Kwat Kwat and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 were both referred to as Whroo and Waveroo, leading to the suggestion that Kwat Kwat is a variety of Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 (Andrews 1920:35; Clark 1996). Additionally, Kwat Kwat was described as a group separate from Bangerang S40 (Tindale 1974:131) or a part of Bangerang S40 (Curr 1887 vol. 3; Bowe & Morey 1999:5).

Sources relating to Bangerang S40 and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang S89 may be relevant.
location_info:
Kwat Kwat is located in the Murray-Goulburn region, VIC. It extends from the southern bank of the Murray River in the north, south to the junction of the King and Ovens rivers near Wangaratta, east to Barnawartha and Indigo Creek, and west to the junction of the Murray and Goulburn rivers (Tindale 1974:206; Cooper & Urry 1981:81).

Neighbouring languages include Wiradjuri D10 to the north, Gundungerre / Yaithmathang S43 to the east, Taungurung S37 to the south and Bangerang S40 to the west.

overview: Oates (1975:06) lists Ngadawanga under Bidungu A40, but the identity of Bidungu is itself uncertain and may not refer to a specific language variety. According to Oates (1975), von Brandenstein reported Ngayawanga (A30) as an alternative name of Bidungu A40, a name which Daisy Bates equated with Ngadawanga. Oates says that Bates reported two dialects of Ngaiawonga (A30): a northern dialect, north of Wiluna, and a southern dialect associated with Lake Way, Wiluna, Mt Sir Samuel and Lawler's Range. Bates's analysis was informed by a body of some texts and a 100-word vocabulary she collected. Oates ventures that Bidungu A40 may be the cover term and Ngaiawanga and Ngadawanga the names of the dialects, though she also notes that Hudson believes Bidungu A40 to be only a geographical term. Note, though, that other dialects are reported for Birdungu. See A40 for details.
location_info: Meekatharra north to Gascoyne River; at Mount Maitland and Robinson Range; east to Wiluna and Lakes Way and King; at Peak Hill and Murchison West (Tindale 1974).

overview:
Jeithi is the name of the Jeithi people from the area north of the Murray River and southwest of Wagga Wagga, NSW. It is also a proposed language name. There is little information about the meaning of the name Jeithi.

According to the Jeithi Jerilderie Aboriginal Corporation and Jeithi Aboriginal Group - Cultural Centre, Jeithi people spoke Bangerang S40. The Jeithi community is generally associated with the towns of Deniliquin and Jerilderie (Gordon in Curr 1887:396-7; Jeithi Aboriginal Group - Cultural Centre 2025). However, there is little information known about Jeithi as a language.

Jeithi is proposed as a separate language variety by Tindale (1974:194), using wordlists provided in Edward M. Curr's 'The Australian Race' (McLean in Curr v.3, 1887:394-5; Gordon in Curr v.3, 1887:396-7). However, Curr (1887:363-4) and linguist Lynette Oates (1975:409) attributed these same wordlists exclusively to Wiradjuri D10.

Linguists Jim Wafer and Amanda Lissarague (2008:222) attempt to resolve this by classifying Jeithi as a third variety of a 'Central NSW language', with the other varieties being Wiradjuri D10 and Wirraayaraay D65. They note that further comparative work using the wordlists provided in Curr (1887) could help to clarify this distinction.
location_info: Jeithi is located roughly between the Murrumbidgee and Murray Rivers, NSW (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:222). The easternmost point is around Howlong, and the westernmost point is around Deniliquin, with the area also extending along the Yanco and Billabong creeks (Tindale 1974:193-194). Yanco, Urana, and Jerilderie are associated with Jeithi (Maclean in Curr v.3 1887:394-5).

overview:
Wangkatha, Wangkatja A103 and Pindiini A102 are all listed as separate dialects of the Western Desert language A80 in this database but they appear to be very close to each other and hardly distinguishable.

Thieberger (1993), Douglas (1990 p.c.) and Glass (1990 p.c.) point out that Wanggatha from around Mt Margaret and Leonora is different to Wangatja which is spoken at Cundelee and Coonana. Glass also notes that the term Wangkatja is confusing, 'because all the Western Desert speaking Aborigines of the Eastern Goldfields and surrounding desert areas call themselves Wangkatja'.

Tindale's Pindiini may be equivalent to Wangkatja A103 or Wangkatha A12 - he lists Wanggada as an alternative name of Pindiini A102. Between Pindiini and Wangkatha, Tindale's map shows two other groups, Murunitja A8 and Tjeraridjal A7, but the validity of these groups is uncertain. Wangatha or Wangkatja A103 may have been spoken there.
location_info: Mt Margaret and Leonora (WA Handbook)

overview:
Previously Andajin was linked to the code K23 and Andidja was treated as an alternative name. Although information is sketchy and McGregor (1988) lists Andidja as a member of the Worrorran language group and an alternative name for Andajin, Saunders (2007 p.c.) believes the two names do not refer to the same language.

Andajin, which appears more recently in the records, is treated as closely related to Ngarinyin K18 by Dixon (2002), McGregor and Rumsey (2009) and McGregor (1988) and is generally associated with the King Leopold Ranges area of Western Australia.

According to Saunders (2007 p.c.), Andajin is in a dialectal relationship with Ngarinyin K18 and Wurla K43. Ngarinyin is described as 'heavy' and Wurla and Andajin are described as 'light'. Andedja K23 appears in the earlier sources (e.g. Elkin 1933, Kabery 1935) and is associated with the Forrest River region.

Glasgow, Hocking and Steiner (nd) say that Andidja K23 has been variously linked to Wumbulgari, Gunin K36, Wunambal K22, and Wuladja. Capell (1963) says it is a dialect of the 'Forrest River' language, along with Gwini K36, Walar K45, Jeidji K32, Manungu K46 and Wembria K31, and Oates (1975) links Andidja / Andidjara K23 to Wunambal K22.

Tindale (1974) does not mention 'Andajin' but associates Andedja / Andidja with two different identities, as a variant name for both Wilawila K35 and Ngarinjin K18. Saunders (p.c.) says both Andajin and Andidja have been referred to as Arawari K28, which is a directional term meaning 'south' or 'south-east'. As K23 was originally assigned to Andidja, this code assignment has been restored and a new record and code for Andajin K64 has been created.
location_info:
... the country around Glenroy and Mornington cattle stations including part of the Fitzroy river, the Adcock river and the lower Hann River (Saunders 2007 p.c.).

The general territorial association extended from the King Leopold Ranges in the south to the eastern Philips Range in the north, from Lungra Yard in the west to around Tharlow Hill in the east. Lungra Yard, Glenroy, Mornington, Sir John Gorge, Fitzroy Gorge, Macnamara Creek were all associated with Andajin (Harvey AILEC 0802).

overview:
Wiradjuri is the language of the Southern West Yiradyuri / Wiradyuri / Wiradjuri People of Central New South Wales. The name Wiradjuri follows the 'no'-'having' structure of many neighbouring language names, with wirraay meaning 'no' and the suffix -dhurray or -juuray meaning 'having' (McNicol & Hosking 1994:79-80, 87). This distinguishes Wiradjuri from similar neighbouring languages.

Wiradjuri is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Wiradjuri was one of the first languages in Australia to receive detailed historical accounts (Capell 1963:16), and a number of valuable dictionaries and learning materials for Wiradjuri have been published from these. Dr Stan Grant Sr, a Wiradjuri Elder and language champion, has published two dictionaries and two grammars in partnership with Dr John Rudder (Grant & Rudder 2001; 2005; 2010; 2014). The Wiradjuri Condobolin Corporation (WCC) Language Program and the Wiradjuri Study Centre also provide a dictionary and learning materials. Furthermore, various primary schools on Wiradjuri Country began teaching Wiradjuri language programs in the early 2000s. NSW TAFE and Charles Sturt University began offering certificate programs in Wiradjuri language and culture in the 2010s.

Wiradjuri is part of the Central-NSW group within the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023:lxxxiv). The other languages in this group include Ngiyampaa / Ngempa D22, Wayilwan D20, Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23, Yuwaalayaay D54, and Yuwaalaraay D27. Wiradjuri itself can be divided into roughly two main varieties according to researchers Dianne Hosking and Sally McNicol (1993:3) - a Northern variety, and a Southern variety.
location_info:
Wiradjuri is located within a large area in Central New South Wales, with a northernmost point around Dubbo, and southernmost around Albury (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:221). Hay, Booligal, and Condobolin are westernmost localities, and Mudgee, Bathurst, Cowra, and Gundagai are easternmost localities (Tindale 1974:201).

Neighbouring languages include Gamilaraay / Gamilaroi / Kamilaroi D23 to the north, Ngyiampaa / Ngempa D22 to the west, and Ngarigu / Ngarigo S46 to the east.

overview:
According to WA Handbook, von Brandenstein said that Tjarrgudi (A56) was the name commonly used for both Kartujarra A51 and Purtijarra A54.

Oates and Oates (1970:72) report that von Brandenstein collected data from speakers at Jigalong. See also Western Desert language A80.
location_info: Inland west of Robertson Range, head of Oakover River (Davidson according to Oates 1975:105)

overview: This is a dialect of Wergaia S17 according to Clark (2005:21-22). Documentation on Wergaia S17 may be relevant.
location_info: ... between Boorung and Morton Plain (Clark 2005:21) [The map, Victorian Aboriginal Corporation for Languages. 2006. Aboriginal Languages of Victoria shows Wotjobaluk being south of Lake Tyrell]

overview:
There is disagreement between sources regarding the final nasal - Tjuparn, Tjupany and Tjupan. Tindale includes Tjupun in his list of alternate names for Pini A25. 

Hanson (Wangka Maya 2008) says that Tjupan (A31) has been referred to as 'Tjalkati', 'Kuwarra' and 'Kurlujarra'.

Liberman (1978) treats Tjupany as a dialect of the Western Desert language A80 but he also questions whether it refers to a separate dialect.

Horton treats Tjupany (A31) and Kuwarra A16 as distinct dialects of Western Desert language A80. Von Brandenstein made some recordings at Meekatharra and Marsh is doing a depth study (Oates & Oates 1970:79). See the Goldfields Aboriginal Language Centre  https://wangka.com.au/tjupan/.
location_info: Possibly Meekatharra according to Oates and Oates description (Oates & Oates 1970:79) North of Yellirrie, Mt. Russell, Mt. Yagahong, west of Meekatharra, east of Wiluna on Liberman's map (Liberman 1978) (Berndt's map (1959) shows Djuban to be south of Lake Carnegie. The mapping of this language in AUSTLANG follows Liberman.) north of Mulga Queen (Berndt 1959, in Wangka Maya PALC 2008) Tjupan people are originally from the Wiluna area, from Darlot, Carnegie, Wongawol and Sandstone areas, and possibly through to the Menzies area. (Wangka Maya PALC 2008) Contemporary location Many Tjupan people have migrated to other locations throughout the Goldfield's regions. (Wangka Maya PACL 2008)

overview: Walmalbarra is only known from a vocabulary in Roth (1900 in Dixon 1982); this is a dialect of Dyirbal Y123 (Dixon (1982, 2002). Documentation on Dyirbal Y123 may be relevant.

Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang is the language of the Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang people of the Ovens and Kiewa Valley region, VIC. Waywurru is the language of the Pallanganmiddang people, however both names have been used interchangeably to refer to language and people (Eira 2008:152). The two main preferred spellings are represented in the language name heading.

The name Waywurru may follow a common pattern of many Australian language names, with way meaning 'no' and the suffix -wurru meaning 'mouth' or 'tongue' (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:69). However, this is unconfirmed.

Pallanganmiddang may also follow a common pattern, with the suffix -midhang meaning 'mouth' or 'tongue' (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:69). However, the meaning of pallangan is unknown (Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:69).

Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang traditional groups include Pallanganmiddang and Tare-re-mittung (Clark 2005; Clark 2011; Waywurru Women's Collective 2026).

Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang is undergoing community-led language revitalisation. Dhudhuroa S44 and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang have collaborated on language revitalisation work, including the Waywurru and Dhudhuroa Language Program which operated in Wodonga, VIC (Eira 2008:152; Wafer & Lissarrague 2008:65).

Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang is a language of the Pama-Nyungan language family (Bowern 2023). It is a member of the Eastern Victoria language group, along with Kurnai S68 and Dhudhuroa S44 (Bowern 2023). The relationship between Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang and neighbouring languages is uncertain (Bowe & Morey 1999:17).

The relationship between Kwat Kwat S97, Bangerang S40 and Waywurru / Pallanganmiddang has been debated. Kwat Kwat S97 was previously listed under Bangerang S40, formally 'Bangerang / Kwat Kwat / Waveroo'.
